usable.claim: WHO defines burn-out as a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with three dimensions: exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. WHO says it is not classified as a medical condition and applies only to the occupational context.
usable.values: Three dimensions. WHO quote: should not be applied to describe experiences in other areas of life. Code QD85, chapter 24, and exclusions (mood, anxiety, stress-associated and adjustment disorders) were read on a third-party ICD mirror, https://findacode.com/icd-11/code-129180281.html, not on the WHO browser.
usable.source: World Health Organization (2019). Burn-out an occupational phenomenon: International Classification of Diseases.
usable.population: Definition for classification use; not an empirical sample.
usable.implication: An exhaustion-only index cannot be called a burnout index. The app needs energy, distance and efficacy signals, must not use diagnostic language, and should name exhaustion for non-workers rather than burnout. A user-logged 'burnout day' is a self-label, not a clinical event.
usable.note: I opened the WHO page. It gives the three dimensions, says burn-out is not classified as a medical condition, and uses the quoted wording about other areas of life. The WHO page does not state QD85 or the chapter number. The findacode mirror confirms QD85, chapter 24, and the four exclusions (anxiety/fear, mood, adjustment, stress-associated). The WHO ICD browser returned only navigation, so the code is still mirror-only, as the claim says.

usable.claim: BAT authors treat structured, goal-directed, mandatory activity as 'work', so students can have burnout, but homemakers, retirees and the unemployed as such cannot. This is the authors' position and is broader than WHO's wording. A student BAT-S exists, with limited cross-sectional validation and no Korean version.
usable.values: BAT-S here: 12 items, 1 to 5 scale; total omega .874; mental distance alpha .652, the weakest. Student questionnaire languages on the official site: Dutch, English, Russian, Farsi, Thai. Manual: https://burnoutassessmenttool.be/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Test-Manual-BAT-English-version-2.0-1.pdf ; language list: https://burnoutassessmenttool.be/handleiding_vragenlijst_eng/
usable.source: Carmona-Halty M et al. (2024). Burnout Assessment Tool for Students (BAT-S): evidence of validity in a Chilean sample. Front Psychol 15:1434412. Also Schaufeli, De Witte & Desart, BAT Test Manual v2.0, section 4.5.
usable.population: 461 Chilean undergraduates (70.9% women). Earlier studies per the paper: 745 Italian middle-school students, 399 Romanian undergraduates.
usable.implication: Showing a burnout-style signal to students is defensible only via this broader view, and should be labelled as such. There is no validated Korean student BAT to embed, and adapting the wording conflicts with the no-modification term in I10. Copy for students should talk about study exhaustion rather than occupational burnout.
usable.note: Test Manual section 4.5 (PDF text extracted) says work means structured, goal-directed, mandatory activity. It names athletes, volunteers and students as possibly burning out, and says housewives/men, retirees and the unemployed 'cannot suffer from burnout'. Carmona-Halty 2024 confirmed: 12 items, 1-5 scale, omega .874, mental distance alpha .652 (omega .689), n=461, 70.9% female, plus the earlier 745 Italian and 399 Romanian samples. The official language list shows five student languages and no Korean student form. That paper does not itself define student work; the definition comes from the manual.

usable.claim: The MBI License to Administer and the Transform data licence are research-only, and the former bars individual feedback. Individual feedback is sold separately as Mind Garden Individual Reports ($15 each, hosted on Transform; hosting minimum 20 licences). I found no public licence that permits embedding items in a free third-party app, but no page explicitly addresses apps.
usable.values: $2.75 per administration at the minimum of 50, $0.39 at 50,000. Each opening of the survey counts as one administration. Licence quote: for data collection only and not for providing individual feedback. The page does not mention apps or commercial use.
usable.source: Mind Garden, Inc. MBI License to Administer, product page.
usable.population: Not applicable (licence terms).
usable.implication: Exclude the MBI and do not paraphrase its items. Each daily or monthly opening would be billable, and showing a score to the user breaches the stated licence. Any app use would need a separately negotiated licence from Mind Garden.
usable.note: Every number and term is right for the MBI License to Administer: $2.75 at minimum 50, $0.39 at 50,000, research purposes only, no individual feedback, no open web, each survey opening counts. But 'the public licences' overgeneralises from one page. The page links Transform survey hosting as an alternative licence, and that page sells Individual Reports at $15 each for developmental use. So paid individual feedback does exist, through Mind Garden's own hosting. Neither page mentions apps or commercial use. Inability to embed in a free app is an inference, not a stated term, though a reasonable one. Get legal or Mind Garden confirmation before relying on it.

usable.claim: The page states 22 items for HSS and ES and 16 for GS. It gives no item count for HSS(MP) or GS(S), so '22 items' for HSS(MP) is not from this source.
usable.values: Forms: HSS, HSS(MP), ES 22 items; GS 16 items; GS(S) for students. Korean listed for HSS, HSS(MP), GS, not ES or GS(S). Five profiles: burnout, overextended, ineffective, disengaged, engaged. Reprint: https://www.physicianleaders.org/articles/how-to-measure-burnout-accurately-and-ethically . Publisher and developer are an interested party, but here they argue against their own older thresholds.
usable.source: Mind Garden. Maslach Burnout Inventory product page. Maslach C, Leiter MP. How to measure burnout accurately and ethically (HBR article, read via a physician-leader reprint).
usable.population: Publisher and developer statements; norm groups not described on the page.
usable.implication: Show dimension scores or a pattern, not one number on a red line. A profile-style view (for example high exhaustion with intact efficacy) is closer to the construct than a single index, but the profile norms themselves belong to the MBI and cannot be reused.
usable.note: The Mind Garden page confirms cut-offs were removed for lack of diagnostic validity, the older ones were arbitrary thirds of the norm population, it is 'not a clinical diagnostic tool', Korean is listed for HSS, HSS(MP) and GS, and the five profiles. The physicianleaders.org piece confirms Maslach and Leiter reject summed scores and exhaustion-only use. It carries a 2021 Harvard Business School Publishing notice. The page also says profiles were validated only for the MBI-GS.

usable.claim: The absence of an accepted diagnostic standard means sensitivity and specificity of burnout measures could not be measured. Among the five measures reviewed, the CBI appeared most valid and the OLBI second, mainly on content validity. Responsiveness was reported as never assessed.
usable.values: 19 studies; COSMIN appraisal. The discussion also lists very-low-quality CBI responsiveness evidence, which is inconsistent with the results section.
usable.source: Shoman Y, Marca SC, Bianchi R, Godderis L, van der Molen HF, Guseva Canu I (2021). Psychometric properties of burnout measures: a systematic review. Epidemiol Psychiatr Sci 30:e8.
usable.population: 19 validation studies: MBI 15, and BM, PBI, OLBI, CBI one each. Literature to September 2018. BAT and SMBM not covered.
usable.implication: Every default threshold is provisional. There is no gold standard for calling a person burned out, so the personal model is not a luxury add-on, and its 'event' label will itself be imperfect.
usable.note: Shoman 2021 confirmed: 19 studies (MBI 15; BM, PBI, OLBI, CBI one each), search to 27 September 2018, COSMIN with GRADE, sensitivity and specificity precluded by no accepted diagnostic standard. It reads 'CBI appeared the most valid' and OLBI 'second most valid', with CBI validated in one study only. The Results/Discussion inconsistency on CBI responsiveness is real. SMBM is explicitly outside the assessment; BAT is not mentioned.

usable.claim: The CBI is the only measure found with an explicit official statement allowing commercial use. NFA, the Danish institute that hosts it, says it may be used freely for non-commercial and commercial purposes if the source is clearly cited.
usable.values: Required citation: Borritz M et al. Burnout among employees in human service work: design and baseline findings of the PUMA study. Scand J Public Health 2006;34:49-58. Contact named on the page: Prof. Thomas Clausen, NFA. No fee or request is mentioned. The page is silent on adaptation and translation.
usable.source: National Research Centre for the Working Environment (NFA), Denmark. Copenhagen Burnout Inventory - CBI page (updated 07-10-2026).
usable.population: Not applicable (licence terms).
usable.implication: CBI is the lowest-risk instrument to embed in a free app, and displaying items appears permitted. Show the citation in the app. Because modification and translation are not covered, ask NFA by email before changing wording, for example replacing 'work' with 'study'.
usable.note: NFA page: 'may be used freely for non-commercial and commercial purposes, provided that the following source is clearly cited'. The Borritz 2006 citation matches and Thomas Clausen is the named contact. No fee, request, adaptation or translation is mentioned. 'Sidst opdateret: 07-10-2026' is confirmed; the date format is ambiguous. 'Only measure found' reflects this claim set; I could not re-search it because the web search limit was reached. Silence on translation means Korean translation rights are unresolved, not granted.

usable.claim: The minimum-items rule is at least 3 of 6 for personal and client, and at least 4 of 7 for work, so slightly more than half on the work scale.
usable.values: Personal burnout, Danish sample: mean 32.7, SD 15.7, alpha .80. Employed 31.7 (14.8); not employed 36.6 (18.3). PUMA: personal 35.9 (16.5), work 33.0 (17.7), client 30.9 (17.6). At or above 50: 22.2%, 19.8%, 15.9%. Scoring steps 0, 25, 50, 75, 100; one work item reversed. A subscale needs at least half its items answered. Authors advise against printing items in the listed order.
usable.source: Borritz M, Kristensen TS (2004). Copenhagen Burnout Inventory: normative data from a representative Danish population and results from the PUMA study.
usable.population: Danish adults aged 20-59 (N=1,498, 75% response, telephone); PUMA: 1,917 Danish human service workers, 83% women.
usable.implication: Treat 50 as a conventional default and show its origin. Roughly one in five Danish human service workers exceed it, so it marks elevated exhaustion, not a burnout case. Danish means give context only, not a Korean norm. The personal subscale has no work wording, so it fits students and non-workers better than the other two.
usable.note: PDF text extracted. All figures match: 19 items (6+7+6), 0-100 item averages, 32.7/15.7/.80, 31.7/14.8, 36.6/18.3, PUMA means and SDs, 22.2/19.8/15.9% at 50 or above, N=1,498, 75% response, telephone, ages 20-59, PUMA 1,917 with 83% women. 'Defined as 50 points or more' appears only as a descriptive definition, with no validation. Only the personal scale has national norms.

usable.claim: The CBI self-test is a developer-issued form with action-worded bands written for self-scoring, with no derivation given. It is not the only free instrument with individual bands: the BAT user manual also issues them, ROC-derived against clinical groups. The top band tells people to seek help at once to change their situation.
usable.values: Personal and client scales, sum 0-24: 0-5, 6-11, 12-17, 18+. Work scale, sum 0-28: 0-6, 7-13, 14-20, 21+. Bands read: no signs; things to watch; symptoms to act on; so exhausted that help should be sought at once. By my arithmetic these equal 25, 50 and 75 on the 0-100 scale, i.e. equal quarters, which suggests convention rather than data. Danish national mean on the personal sum: 7.7.
usable.source: Borritz M, Kristensen TS. CBI self-test (Danish), NFA.
usable.population: Comparison values from about 2,000 PUMA participants, Danish human service workers.
usable.implication: Usable as default CBI bands, labelled as developer convention. The strongest band's advice to seek help could anchor a help-resources screen. Softer wording is advisable because the band has no criterion validation.
usable.note: The self-test PDF text confirms the purpose (individual self-rating), all bands, national mean 7.7 and the PUMA comparison of about 2,000. The arithmetic is right: 6/12/18 of 24 and 7/14/21 of 28 equal 25/50/75. No derivation is given. The word 'only' fails: the BAT user manual, also free, gives green/orange/red bands and says cut-offs play an important role in individual assessment. The top band means seeking help to change your situation, not specifically clinical care.

usable.claim: The population is homecare workers for older adults (care workers serving older people; ages 33-72, mean 56.76), not 'older homecare workers' as such.
usable.values: Original 3-factor: CFI .866, RMSEA .112. Refined 18 items: CFI .924, RMSEA .091. Two-factor 12 items (personal plus client): CFI .950, RMSEA .084. Work subscale correlated above .85 with the others. Composite reliability .90 to .92. Means: personal 38.59 (18.52), work 33.94 (17.81), client 34.88 (18.36). At or above 50: 30.4%, 23.3%, 26.9%. Questionnaire supplied as S1 Fig. The article mentions no permission from CBI authors.
usable.source: Jeon G-S, You S-J, Kim M-G, Kim Y-M, Cho S-I (2019). Psychometric properties of the Korean version of the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory in Korean homecare workers for older adults. PLoS ONE 14(8):e0221323.
usable.population: 464 Korean homecare workers, mean age 56.76 years, 30.88 work hours per week, 2016.
usable.implication: Korean wording is available as a starting point, ideally the personal subscale. Validity in Korean students and developers is unknown, so Korean scores need the app's own baseline rather than a transported Danish or homecare mean.
usable.note: All fit indices, reliabilities, means and proportions match Jeon 2019. The dropped item is work item 4, the only reversed item, with a loading of .16 (Results) or .19 (Discussion). Authors call the original fit inadequate and recommend the two-factor model for homecare workers. No test-retest and no permission statement. The paper says first among homecare workers in Korea, not first in Korea. 'Only validation found' was not re-searched because of the search limit.

usable.claim: The site wording is 'Only academic or substantive questions will be answered', not academic only.
usable.values: Quote: may be used free of charge without requesting permission from the authors. Required citation: Schaufeli, Desart & De Witte (2020), IJERPH 17:9495. The user manual says the BAT may be integrated into an online platform with automatic scores, but its copyright page bars reproducing that publication without written permission. Site says the author address answers only academic questions.
usable.source: Burnout Assessment Tool official site, English start page, KU Leuven authors.
usable.population: Not applicable (licence terms).
usable.implication: BAT is usable in a free app at fixed wording, scale and scoring. Any reworded, daily-window or item-subset version falls outside the stated terms. Confirm in writing whether displaying items in a PWA is fine, given the manual's copyright line. If a fee is ever charged, recheck.
usable.note: The start page confirms non-proprietary, free without requesting permission, 'should not be modified', and the citation. It is silent on commercial use. The user manual allows online integration with automatic scores and carries the all-rights-reserved notice, as does the test manual. The instrument itself is said to be non-proprietary, so the manual copyright may cover the manual text rather than the items, but neither source settles this. The no-modification term is what matters for rewording or subsetting items.

usable.claim: The BAT has 23 items in four core dimensions (exhaustion, mental distance, cognitive impairment, emotional impairment), scored as a 1 to 5 mean. A 12-item short form exists. The authors state it must not be used for diagnosis or to separate burnout from depression.
usable.values: BAT-23: exhaustion 8, mental distance 5 (4 in the general version), cognitive 5, emotional 5, plus 10 optional secondary symptoms. BAT-12: 3 per dimension. Flemish total-core: green to 2.58, orange 2.59-3.01, red 3.02+. BAT-12: green to 2.53, orange 2.54-2.95, red 2.96+. Non-working BAT-23 total: same 2.59 and 3.02. No BAT-12 total cutoff for the general version. Norm bands: lowest 25%, highest 25%, top 5%. Manual copy found on a third-party host; the official site lists the same manual.
usable.source: Schaufeli WB, De Witte H, Desart S. User Manual, Burnout Assessment Tool, version 2.0 (July 2020). KU Leuven.
usable.population: Flemish and Dutch employees; Flemish patients; non-working Flemish individuals for the general version.
usable.implication: BAT is closer to the WHO construct than the current index, and its cognitive and emotional dimensions may suit developers and students, though that fit is my inference. Follow the manual: drop the word 'burnout' from the questionnaire title, use BAT-12 total rather than subscales for individuals, and show a not-a-diagnosis line.
usable.note: User manual text extracted. Principles 1 and 3 bar diagnosis and differential diagnosis, including against depression. Item counts, the Flemish tables, non-working totals (2.59, 3.02), the missing general BAT-12 total cut-off and norm bands all match. The word 'optional' for secondary symptoms is not the manual's; it says they are always added together and interpreted as a whole. The general version totals 22 items and its mental distance items still refer to work. For individual assessment the manual prefers the full version and recommends only the BAT-12 total, with subscale orange optional.

usable.claim: Pooled BAT cutoffs were derived by ROC against clinician-assessed burnout groups in three European samples: orange at the maximum Youden index, red at specificity of about .90. The authors call them preliminary and tell users to apply them tentatively.
usable.values: BAT-23 orange 2.59 (sens .92, spec .79), red 3.02 (sens .74, spec .91). BAT-12 orange 2.54 (.89, .79), red 2.96 (.71, .89). AUC about .91. Exhaustion 3.06 and 3.31, AUC .92. Mental distance AUC .76, red sensitivity .30. BAT-12 subscale cutoffs not given.
usable.source: Schaufeli WB et al. (2023). How to assess severe burnout? Cutoff points for the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT) based on three European samples. Scand J Work Environ Health.
usable.population: Employees: Netherlands 1,370, Flanders 1,403, Finland about 1,372. Burnout groups: 335, 158, 50. Belgian group partly self-reported diagnosis.
usable.implication: These are the best-derived defaults available, for BAT total scores only. About a fifth of healthy controls fall above orange at spec .79, so orange means 'worth attention'. Clinical samples were on sick leave or in care, so red is not an early warning, and neither line applies to GrowLog's own 1 to 5 mood items.
usable.note: PMC full text: all cut-offs, sensitivities, specificities and AUCs match. Samples 1,370/1,403/1,372; burnout groups 335 (table says 334), 158, 50. Red required specificity of at least .90, and orange used Youden. 'Preliminary and should therefore be used tentatively' confirmed. In Belgium about 67 of 158 were clinically interviewed and 91 were self-reported diagnoses, so 'clinician-assessed' does not hold for that group, as the claim notes. BAT-12 subscale cut-offs are not given. All samples are European workers.

usable.claim: Swedish cut-offs were 'somewhat lower' than those of the other three European countries. Pooled versus Swedish classification differed significantly (BAT23 Z=14.11, BAT12 Z=17.44, P<.0001; agreement 87.6% and 81.0%), and pooled cut-offs placed 12.4% and 19% of respondents in a lower risk group.
usable.values: BAT23 orange 2.41 (sens .92, spec .80), red 2.80 (.69, .91). BAT12 orange 2.21 (.91, .74), red 2.71 (.60, .91). BAT4 orange 2.38 (.93, .72), red 3.13 (.47, .93). About 13% of the workforce were red. Self-recruited patients and possible later-stage burnout are stated caveats.
usable.source: Hadzibajramovic E, Dahlqvist I, Jonsdottir IH, De Witte H (2026). Clinical and screening utility of the Burnout Assessment Tool: a comparative evaluation of BAT23, BAT12 and BAT4 in Sweden. Scand J Work Environ Health 52(3):263-271.
usable.population: Swedish workforce N=1,603; healthy employees N=1,162; self-recruited exhaustion disorder group N=159, 25 with confirmed diagnosis.
usable.implication: Thresholds move by about 0.2 to 0.3 between neighbouring European countries, so a Belgian line cannot be assumed to fit Korea. Show default BAT lines as approximate ranges, and let personal history outweigh them over time.
usable.note: All cut-offs, sensitivities, specificities, the 13% red share (13.3% and 12.6%), BAT4 red non-recommendation, samples and caveats match. The authors do prioritise country-specific cut-offs. 'Significantly lower' is not what they say: their wording is 'somewhat lower'. The significance test was a marginal homogeneity test on classification agreement, not on the cut-off values. 'No Korean cut-offs' was not re-searched because of the search limit.

usable.claim: The 4-item BAT4 has one item per core dimension and is positioned for group or organisational screening, not diagnosis. The development paper set no cutoffs, did not test convergent validity, and warns shortening may reduce power to detect change.
usable.values: Person separation index .64 to .77, .72 pooled. Rasch fit failed in Austria and Japan. Results in logits; no sum-score procedure described. Authors recommend BAT23 for clinical use.
usable.source: Hadzibajramovic E, Schaufeli W, De Witte H (2024). The ultra-short version of the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT4). PLoS ONE.
usable.population: National samples from Netherlands, Flanders, Austria, Germany, Finland, Ireland, Japan, Czech Republic. Korea not included.
usable.implication: BAT4 fits a short recurring check better than BAT23 on burden, but individual precision is modest and no study tests weekly repetition. Use it to trigger a fuller check rather than as a personal score of record.
usable.note: PLOS full text confirms one item per dimension, group screening and 'not as a diagnostic tool', no cut-offs, no convergent validity test, 'lower power to detect change', PSI .64-.77 and .72 pooled, Austria and Japan misfit (authors note large-sample sensitivity), logit results, and long version for clinical settings. Eight countries, no Korea. The later Swedish study does add BAT4 cut-offs.

usable.claim: Full text is available at https://accesson.kr/ksiop/assets/pdf/19994/journal-33-4-461.pdf . Reliability is reported there, and the official K-BAT PDF has 23 core items, one more than Cho's final form.
usable.values: 22 of 23 items retained. Convergent, external discriminant and criterion validity reported as supported. No reliability figures on the page; no test-retest mentioned. The official site hosts a Korean work-related PDF labelled K-BAT: https://burnoutassessmenttool.be/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/BAT-Korean.pdf . It matches Cho's pre-analysis translation: 21 of Cho's 22 retained items are identical, item 3 differs by one particle, item 7 by spacing only, and item 9 (dropped by Cho) is present (checked 2026-11, see I26).
usable.source: Cho S-H (2020). A preliminary validation study for the Korean version of the Burnout Assessment Tool (K-BAT). Korean J Ind Organ Psychol 33(4):461-499.
usable.population: South Korean office workers: 367 for EFA, a further 345 for CFA.
usable.implication: Use the Korean file hosted on the official BAT site to stay within the no-modification term. Treat Korean scores as uncalibrated: there are no Korean norms or cutoffs, and the validated form may differ by one item from the 23-item scoring tables.
usable.note: The abstract page confirms all stated points. The linked PDF is open and readable, so more is verifiable than the claim says. Item 9 (mental distance) was dropped, leaving 8+4+5+5=22. Alphas at N=345: total .94, EX .91, MD .84, CC .87, EC .85. K-BAT mean 2.46 (SD .62). No test-retest found. The official PDF is labelled K-BAT and numbers 23 core plus 10 secondary items, so its count does not match Cho's final 22-item form. Whether it uses Cho's wording is still unverified. The 345 were public-corporation office workers.

usable.claim: Scoring is visible: KBOSS has 12 items, 4 per dimension, with cut-offs exhaustion at or above 21, cynicism at or above 18, inefficacy at or above 15. Above cut-off: 13.8%, 8.7%, 30.7%. Exhaustion alone therefore flags about four times the three-dimension rate. Paper: https://ijomeh.eu/pdf-211458-132073?filename=Relationship-between-job-.pdf
usable.values: 3.3%, about 34 cases by my calculation. High overall job stress OR 17.56 (95% CI 1.40-220.76), a very wide interval. Abstract only. Scoring and licence not visible.
usable.source: Kim J-H, Park S-G, Yang S-C, Kim H-C, Hwang S-H (2025). Relationship between job stress and burnout among Korean workers in small and medium-sized enterprises. Int J Occup Med Environ Health 38(5):528-44.
usable.population: 1,024 employees of Korean firms with 50-299 workers using outsourced occupational health services.
usable.implication: How the definition is set changes the count a great deal: all three dimensions gives about 3%, exhaustion alone over 20%. A multi-dimension rule would alert far less often than the current index. KBOSS may be worth contacting its authors about, but its licence is unknown.
usable.note: Full text PDF is open, so 'abstract only' is out of date. Confirmed: 1,024 employees, 34 cases (3.3%), Q4 versus Q1 OR 17.56 (1.40-220.76), all three dimensions required. The paper makes no comparison with other instruments' cut-offs, so 'far below' is the researcher's inference, though its own Table 5 supports it. The sample is 80.7% male, 63.3% production jobs, 53.6% response. No licence for the scale is stated; the instrument paper is its ref 13 (Kim HD et al., Saf Health Work 2021;12(4):522-529), which I did not open.

usable.claim: The OLBI has 16 items on exhaustion and disengagement, with no efficacy dimension, so it does not cover WHO's third dimension. No official licence statement was found, and published researchers obtained permission from Demerouti directly. Cutoffs circulate but their primary derivation was not verified.
usable.values: Scale 1 to 4, half reversed, total 16-64. Cutoffs seen only second hand in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.14357 : at or above 2.25 exhaustion and 2.1 disengagement; 2.85 and 2.6 in a working sample; 3.13 and 2.72 clinical; total 35 of 64. Student form: 14 items in Brazil and Portugal, exhaustion alpha .565, not invariant across countries (https://www.scielo.br/j/prc/a/7zgKNFznCFY6wTS4HvKGWMR/). No Korean validation found.
usable.source: Xu H et al. (2022). Reliability and validity of the Chinese version of Oldenburg Burnout Inventory for Chinese nurses. Nursing Open 9:320-328. Cutoffs as listed in arXiv:2409.14357.
usable.population: 641 Chinese nurses for the validation (n from search result); cutoff provenance not verified at primary level.
usable.implication: Do not embed the OLBI without written permission, and treat its numeric cutoffs as weak. Its value is as evidence that day-level exhaustion can be measured (I21), not as a default threshold.
usable.note: Xu 2022 confirmed: 16 items, 8+8, scale 1-4, 8 reversed, range 16-64, 641 nurses (97.97% women), permission from Demerouti, and no cut-off established. arXiv 2409.14357 (Kurpicz-Briki et al.) lists the same cut-offs and cites Peterson 2008, Demerouti 2019 and Summers 2020; those primaries were not opened, so derivation stays unverified. The arXiv paper anchors its scale in the opposite direction to Xu, so check scoring direction before using any cut-off. OLBI-S confirmed: 14 items, alpha .565, not invariant. No licence and no Korean version were not re-searched because of the search limit.

usable.claim: Sundstrom suggests SMBM-11 or SMBM-6 for repeated measures, not the 6-item alone. SMBM-11 cut-off 4.00, sensitivity 95.3%, specificity 93.3%. 'Reviews' is one review.
usable.values: Quote: noncommercial educational or research purposes only. SMBM-22 cutoff 4.00, sens 96.0%, spec 90.0%. SMBM-6 3.75, sens 94.6%, spec 95.0%, general population 17.4%, primary care 71.1%. SMBQ-18 cut 4.4 at the distribution intersection, 83.4% and 86.5% correct, derived and evaluated in the same sample. Review: no test-retest, responsiveness or minimal important change. Review URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11427641/ ; Swedish URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11747081/ ; 4.4 URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3307433/ . No Korean version found.
usable.source: SMBM and SMVM notice to potential users, reproduced in a Hebrew scale sheet at mta.ac.il. Figueiredo S et al. (2024), J Patient Rep Outcomes 8:108. Sundstrom AE et al. (2025), Stress and Health 41(1):e70001. Lundgren-Nilsson A et al. (2012), BMC Public Health.
usable.population: Licence: not applicable, third-party copy of the notice. Sweden: 149 exhaustion disorder patients, 60 controls, 3,406 general population. Review: 5 studies, health professionals.
usable.implication: Skip the SMBM. A self-improvement app is not clearly educational or research use, and a local-only app cannot share sample statistics with the authors. Its 30-working-day recall also fits poorly with short-cycle tracking.
usable.note: Notice text extracted: noncommercial educational or research only, 'no one is charging anyone a fee', and sharing results is a stated condition. Sundstrom values match (22-item 4.00, 96.0/90.0; 6-item 3.75, 94.6/95.0; 17.4%; 71.1%). Figueiredo says 'should not be utilized for clinical purposes', with no test-retest, responsiveness or MIC, in a single review of five studies. Four of those mixed healthcare workers with others. Lundgren-Nilsson confirms 4.4, 83.4% above and 86.5% below, same samples; its 'general' sample was 319 health care and social insurance workers. No Korean version was not re-searched.

usable.claim: This study compared the item only with one MBI:EE item (a three-item MBI:EE was similar). Earlier small studies did compare it with the full MBI:EE: Rohland (n=307), r .64; Hansen and Girgis (n=740), r .68 or .66 (the paper gives both). Expect weaker agreement than r .79 against a full scale.
usable.values: Five ordered categories; burnout at category 3 or higher. AUC .93, sensitivity 83.2%, specificity 87.4%, r .79, kappa .70. Reference is a single MBI item at once a week or more, not a clinical diagnosis. Authors describe the item as non-proprietary and free; no formal licence text found.
usable.source: Dolan ED, Mohr D, Lempa M et al. (2015). Using a single item to measure burnout in primary care staff: a psychometric evaluation. J Gen Intern Med 30(5):582-587.
usable.population: 5,404 US Veterans Health Administration primary care staff, about 25% response, 2012.
usable.implication: A single periodic self-rating is defensible as the 'did burnout arrive' label for personal calibration. It captures exhaustion-weighted self-perception only, needs a Korean translation of unknown validity, and its wording is work-framed, so student wording would be a new, unvalidated variant.
usable.note: All figures match Dolan 2015: N=5,404, about 25% response, May-June 2012, AUC .93, 83.2/87.4, r .79, kappa .70, burnout at 3 or higher, no licensing fee, no test-retest. Literally true of that study, because the full MBI:EE was not in the dataset, but 'never' misleads. The paper cites earlier full-scale comparisons, and those show weaker agreement than the headline figures. A three-item MBI:EE gave similar results here.

usable.claim: BAT scores are moderately stable over months, which allows monthly repetition without implying a fixed trait, but no responsiveness study or minimal important change was found. The manual's statement that variation shows sensitivity to change is an inference, not a test.
usable.values: 6-month r: exhaustion .71 and .75; total core .74 and .73. 1-year: total core .68, exhaustion .69. BAT-12 subscales .55 to .70 at 6 months. Japan 1-month: core .64, secondary .71 (https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01819/full). Manual has no criterion for sufficient stability.
usable.source: Schaufeli WB, De Witte H, Desart S. BAT Test Manual v2.0, section 5.2. Sakakibara K et al. (2020). Validation of the Japanese version of the BAT. Front Psychol.
usable.population: 964 Flemish online respondents (50% dropout over one year); 485 Japanese full-time employees, healthy sample.
usable.implication: A monthly formal check is the most defensible cadence. With no minimal important change, personal change rules must come from the user's own variability, such as a smallest-detectable-change estimate from their history, not a published delta.
usable.note: Test Manual section 5.2 confirmed: exhaustion .71/.75, total core .74/.73, 1-year .69/.68, BAT-12 subscales .55-.70, 50% dropout, no criterion for sufficient stability, and the sensitivity-to-change sentence is an inference. Pairs were N=597/368/447, and the sample came through a Flemish burnout website, so it is self-selected. Sakakibara confirmed: 1 month, .64 and .71, 485 retest of 982, healthy employees. Monthly repetition is the researcher's inference, not a source statement. 'No responsiveness study found' was not re-searched because of the search limit.

usable.claim: Both models fit reasonably, with the two-factor model marginally better on AIC, BIC and SABIC. The authors still prefer one factor as 'more valid' because exhaustion and disengagement correlate .94 within-person and disengagement reliability is low (.66).
usable.values: ICC exhaustion .41, disengagement .45, so 59% and 55% within-person. Within-person omega: exhaustion .81, disengagement .66; single factor .85. Eight negatively worded items, 5-point scale. Cross-level invariance failed. Authors call the findings preliminary. Companion URL: https://www.dovepress.com/burnout-as-a-state-random-intercept-cross-lagged-relationship-between--peer-reviewed-article-PRBM
usable.source: Basinska BA, Gruszczynska E (2020). Burnout as a state. Psychol Res Behav Manag 13:267-278. Gruszczynska E, Basinska BA, Schaufeli WB (2021). PLoS ONE 16(5):e0251257.
usable.population: 235 Polish public administration employees, 73-75% women; 10 consecutive workdays after work.
usable.implication: Never score a day against a trait cutoff such as BAT 2.59. Keep separate models: a daily exhaustion state and a monthly burnout level. Personal alerts should rest on rolling averages, since single days are mostly fluctuation. The items here are OLBI-derived, so their rights follow I17.
usable.note: Confirmed: ICC .41 and .45, 59% and 55% within-person, omega .81/.66 and .85, eight negative items on a 5-point scale, 235 employees, 73-75% women, 10 workdays, cross-level invariance failed, 'not the same latent variable'. 'Preliminary' appears in the 2020 Dovepress paper, not the 2021 PLOS paper. The final clause reverses the fit result: the one-factor model had slightly higher AIC, BIC and SABIC, meaning marginally worse fit. Table 2's other indices could not be read because it is an image.

usable.claim: A single 1 to 10 rating of current fatigue is a validated daily diary measure, tracking a multi-item fatigue scale closely. It measures fatigue, not burnout.
usable.values: r = .80 with POMS fatigue; multilevel beta .70. Daily sleep complaints r = .45; global fatigue r = .51; job control -.12, n.s. Usable diary rates 72.1-78.5%. Limits: self-report, specific sample.
usable.source: van Hooff MLM, Geurts SAE, Kompier MAJ, Taris TW (2007). How fatigued do you currently feel? Convergent and discriminant validity of a single-item fatigue measure. J Occup Health 49:224-234.
usable.population: 120 Dutch university academic staff, 62% men, mean age 45.2; 9 consecutive days, three times daily.
usable.implication: Closest evidence for GrowLog's single daily energy rating, and the item has no known licence barrier. It supports keeping one fast daily question on fatigue. GrowLog's 1 to 5 energy item is a different format and was not validated in this study, nor in Korean.
usable.note: PDF text extracted. Confirmed: 1-10 report mark, r=.80 with POMS, beta .70, sleep complaints .45, global fatigue .51, job control -.12 n.s., usable diaries 72.1/72.6/78.5%, 120 staff, 62% male, mean age 45.2, 9 days, 3 times daily. The authors conclude it is a valid way to assess daily fatigue, citing limits of self-report and a specific sample. The .80 is computed on mean values across all measurement points, so it is person-level, not within-day tracking. The multilevel beta .70 is the relevant repeated-measures figure.

usable.claim: No opened source states that research or non-profit use is simply allowed. The current route is a permission request through ePROVIDE, and CORC says a licence agreement is required with a fee for some users. For a Korean version, permission goes to the translator, not Dr. Cohen. Check ePROVIDE terms before any decision.
usable.values: Submitting a request is free and does not commit to buying. Translations: the sole intellectual property of the translator. FAQ: https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/stress-immunity-disease-lab/scales/.doc/pssfaqs.doc . CORC says Mapi is exclusive distributor and a user fee applies to some users: https://corc.uk.net/outcome-experience-measures/perceived-stress-scale-pss-10 . The FAQ warns against picking individual items.
usable.source: Cohen lab, Carnegie Mellon University. Scales page and PSS FAQ.
usable.population: Not applicable (licence terms).
usable.implication: File a free ePROVIDE request before shipping any PSS, and separately get the Korean translator's permission. Do not pick single PSS items for the daily stress rating. The existing 1 to 5 daily stress item should stay GrowLog's own, unbranded.
usable.note: Confirmed: profit-making use needs special permission and a nominal charge, larger copyrighted scales need specific permission, requests go through ePROVIDE, submitting is free and non-binding, translations belong to translators, and CORC's distributor and fee statements. The first clause is misapplied: the FAQ's yes for research or educational non-profit answers a question about translating the PSS. Neither the FAQ nor the Scales page gives a general non-profit use grant. The FAQ is dated 17 February 2014 and names ASA plus Cohen, while the current page routes to ePROVIDE. The ePROVIDE instrument page returned no content, so its current terms are unverified.

usable.claim: The unsatisfactory 6-week retest (r=.55) was in a PSS-14 study per Lee's results, not PSS-10.
usable.values: PSS-10, 0-40. 2009: men 15.52 (SD 7.44), women 16.14 (7.56); under 25 16.78 (6.86); 25-34 17.46 (7.31); 35-44 16.38 (7.07). Retest r = .85 at 1 week, .82 at 2 weeks (https://www.cmu.edu/common-cold-project/measures-by-study/psychological-and-social-constructs/stress-measures/perceived-stress.html). Review: PSS-10 met .70 in 4 studies; a 6-week retest was unsatisfactory; PSS-4 retest never tested, and it fared worst (Lee 2012, https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/stress-immunity-disease-lab/scales/pdf/review-of-the-psychmetric-evidence.pdf).
usable.source: Cohen S, Janicki-Deverts D (2012). Who's stressed? Distributions of psychological stress in the United States in probability samples from 1983, 2006, and 2009. J Appl Soc Psychol 42(6):1320-1334. Also Cohen lab FAQ and Common Cold Project measure page.
usable.population: US adult national samples of 2,000 in 2006 and 2009 (online panel); 2,387 in 1983. Retest: 274 adults in the Pittsburgh Cold Studies.
usable.implication: Never show 'high stress' from a PSS line. Use it monthly at most, matching its one-month recall, and compare only with the user's own past scores. Cohen's lab expects shorter recall to be fine but has no data, so a weekly PSS is unvalidated.
usable.note: Table 1 of Cohen 2012 confirms all 2009 means and SDs. 2,000 adults each in 2006 and 2009 (online panel) and 2,387 in 1983 (telephone). FAQ: not diagnostic, no cut-offs, comparisons only within your own sample. Common Cold page: .85 and .82, n=274, past-month window. Lee 2012 confirms PSS-10 in 4 of 4 studies and no PSS-4 retest, with the 4-item form faring worst.

usable.claim: In Korean chronic disease patients, KPSS-10 showed good properties after model modification. KPSS-4 was only marginally acceptable, failing internal consistency and RMSEA while meeting other criteria. Neither result is established for healthy Korean adults or students.
usable.values: Alpha: KPSS-14 .75, KPSS-10 .74, KPSS-4 .55. KPSS-4 RMSEA above .1, 90% CI 0.00-0.25. ICCs above .70. r with CES-D .63, .66, .59. Adolescents: 10-item Korean form, n=1,090, 3-month retest described as acceptable, abstract only (Yoon & Kim 2019, https://www.accesson.kr/healthpsy/v.24/3/569/19359). No Korean normative table found.
usable.source: Lee E-H, Chung BY, Suh C-H, Jung J-Y (2015). Korean versions of the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-14, 10 and 4): psychometric evaluation in patients with chronic disease. Scand J Caring Sci 29:183-192.
usable.population: 402 Korean chronic disease patients, 60.4% women, mean age 58.56; retest in rheumatoid arthritis patients at 1 week.
usable.implication: If a validated stress questionnaire is added, use a Korean PSS-10, not PSS-4, subject to I23. Patient data do not transfer directly to students and developers, so rely on within-person change.
usable.note: All numbers match: alpha .75/.74/.55, RMSEA .11 (0.00-0.25), ICC total .80/.81/.77, CES-D .63/.66/.59, n=402, 60.4% women, age 58.56, 1-week retest, permission from Cohen. Two overstatements. Authors call KPSS-4 'only marginally acceptable', not unacceptable: it failed alpha and RMSEA but passed ICC, concurrent and known-groups validity, and CFI was .98. 'In Korean' stretches a chronic-disease sample. KPSS-10 fit also needed a modified model (original RMSEA .08, NFI .88; modified .07, .91). Yoon and Kim confirmed: n=1,090, 3-month retest acceptable, abstract only. No Korean norms was not re-searched.

usable.claim: Sleep duration defaults come from expert consensus: at least 7 h for adults, 8-10 h for teens 14-17, and 7-8 h for people over 65. Threshold status: a consensus cut-point on a continuous risk gradient, not a biological limit. The statement itself says sleep need varies with genetic, behavioral, medical and environmental factors.
usable.values: Adults: 7 h or more, regularly. NSF: 14-17 y 8-10 h; 18-64 y 7-9 h; over 65 7-8 h, and an hour or two outside the range may suit some people. Over 9 h: uncertain risk, may be appropriate for young adults, people repaying sleep debt, or illness. Method: 15-person panel, modified RAND, about 5,314 articles.
usable.source: Watson NF et al. 2015, AASM/SRS consensus statement, Sleep (full statement read). Age bands from National Sleep Foundation guidance, https://www.thensf.org/how-many-hours-of-sleep-do-you-really-need/ (consumer page summarising the 2015 panel; the primary Hirshkowitz paper was not opened).
usable.population: Healthy adults 18-60 (AASM/SRS). NSF bands: teens 14-17, adults 18-64, over 65. Mostly Western evidence.
usable.implication: Use 7 h (adult) or 8 h (under 18) only as the starting prior for sleep need, chosen by age band. Show it as a guideline, not as a harm line. Do not penalise nights over 9 h, because they may be debt repayment. Replace the prior with an estimated personal need as data accumulates.
usable.note: Opened Watson 2015 (PMC4434546): 7 h or more regularly, adults 18-60, 15 experts, modified RAND, 5,314 articles. Over 9 h may suit young adults, people repaying sleep debt or the ill, and is uncertain for others. Sleep need varies with genetic, behavioral, medical and environmental factors. The NSF page gives 14-17 y 8-10 h, 18-64 y 7-9 h, over 65 7-8 h, and an hour or two either side. I also opened the Hirshkowitz 2015 record in Europe PMC (Sleep Health 1(1):40-43), which the researcher had not; its bands match (teenagers 8-10, adults 7-9, older adults 7-8).

usable.claim: Chronic restriction to 6 h or less in bed produces cumulative, dose-dependent cognitive deficits, while self-rated sleepiness barely tracks them after the first days. Threshold status: dose-response. No safe floor was isolated between 6 and 8 h. In a separate trial a 7 h group also lost speed, then stabilised at a lower level.
usable.values: Van Dongen: 4, 6 or 8 h time in bed for 14 days. Up to 2 nights of total deprivation equivalent at 6 h or less. Lapses near-linear with cumulative wakefulness above 15.84 h (SE 0.73). Sleepiness ratings did not separate 6 h from 4 h. Belenky: 3, 5, 7, 9 h for 7 days; 5 and 7 h groups stabilised at reduced performance and did not recover after 3 nights of 8 h.
usable.source: Van Dongen HPA et al. 2003, Sleep (abstract only). Belenky G et al. 2003, J Sleep Res, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12603781/ (abstract only).
usable.population: Small laboratory samples of healthy volunteers: n=48 aged 21-38 (Van Dongen), n=66 (Belenky). Not workers or students in daily life.
usable.implication: Both studies measured time in bed, which is what the app logs, so the numbers map directly. Compute a rolling 7-14 day sleep debt from logged times rather than trusting energy ratings, because people under-report the deficit. Suggested default (design judgement): flag a 7-day average at or below 6 h in bed, or 1 h or more below personal need.
usable.note: Van Dongen 2003 abstract: n=48, age 21-38, 4/6/8 h for 14 days; up to 2 nights of total deprivation equivalent at 6 h or less; near-linear above 15.84 h (SE 0.73); sleepiness ratings did not separate 6 h from 4 h. Belenky 2003 abstract: n=66, 3/5/7/9 h for 7 days, then 3 days at 8 h; 5 and 7 h groups stabilised at a reduced level with no recovery. Lapses rose only in the 5 h group, so the 7 h loss is in speed. 'No safe floor between 6 and 8 h' is the researcher's inference, not a finding stated in either abstract.

usable.claim: One long night does not clear accumulated sleep debt. After 5 nights at 4 h, deficits improved with longer recovery sleep but some remained even after 10 h in bed. Threshold status: dose-response, with exponential recovery curves for lapses and subjective sleepiness.
usable.values: 142 restricted, 17 controls. One recovery night of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 or 10 h. Incomplete recovery at 10 h for lapses, subjective sleepiness and subjective fatigue. NSF: about 1-2 extra hours per non-work day helps most people recover.
usable.source: Banks S, Van Dongen HPA, Maislin G, Dinges DF 2010, Sleep (abstract only). Catch-up figure from NSF guideline summary, https://www.thensf.org/sleep-schedules-sleep-timing-guideline/ (consensus, not a dose-finding study).
usable.population: 159 healthy adults aged 22-45 in a laboratory; restriction was severe (4 h), so milder debt may behave differently.
usable.implication: Model sleep debt as a stock that decays over several nights, capped per night, and never reset by one lie-in. A cap of 1-2 h credit per night is a defensible default, but it rests on consensus rather than measured kinetics.
usable.note: Banks 2010 abstract: 159 adults aged 22-45, 142 restricted and 17 controls, 5 nights at 4 h, one recovery night of 0-10 h. Recovery was incomplete at 10 h for PVT, KSS and POMS fatigue. Exponential fits apply to PVT and KSS; MWT fit linearly. NSF says 1-2 extra hours on non-work days can benefit most people, which is softer than 'helps most people recover'.

usable.claim: Palmer: 154 studies (1,338 effect sizes), not '154 experiments'.
usable.values: Positive affect SMD -0.27 to -1.14; anxiety SMD 0.57 to 0.63; arousal to emotional stimuli SMD -0.20 to -0.53. Subjective sleep measures related to affect more strongly than actigraphy.
usable.source: Palmer CA et al. 2024, Psychological Bulletin (abstract summary only). Hickman et al. 2024 systematic review of 121 studies, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11280943/fullTextXML (first 100,000 characters read).
usable.population: Palmer: healthy participants aged 7-79, 154 experiments, N=5,717. Hickman: healthy, affective-disorder and shift-work samples using ambulatory monitoring.
usable.implication: Make last night's sleep a lagged predictor of today's energy and mood in the personal model. Expect energy and mood to fall before the stress rating rises. Self-rated sleep quality will correlate with mood partly through shared reporting, so keep duration from logged times as a separate signal.
usable.note: Palmer 2024 (Psychol Bull 150(4):440-463) abstract: 1,338 effect sizes, N=5,717, age 7-79, healthy populations. Positive affect SMD -0.27 to -1.14, anxiety 0.57 to 0.63, blunted arousal -0.20 to -0.53, negative affect mixed, nonlinear effects present. Hickman 2024 (Sensors): 121 studies, associations generally bidirectional, sleep more often the stronger predictor of later affect, stronger for self-report than actigraphy. Only slip: the abstract says 154 studies, not experiments.

usable.claim: Add that the fully adjusted Windred models used N=46,721, not the full ~60,977.
usable.values: All-cause mortality top vs bottom regularity quintile: HR 0.70 (0.59-0.83) fully adjusted. Best duration quintile: HR 0.76 (0.65-0.89). Fang: variability in sleep time b=0.4 and wake time b=0.081 with PHQ-9; mean and variability each r2=0.01. Within person, smaller day-to-day shifts predicted better next-day mood.
usable.source: Windred DP et al. 2024, Sleep (first 100,000 of 162,000 characters read). Fang Y et al. 2021, npj Digit Med, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22Day-to-day%20variability%20in%20sleep%20parameters%20and%20depression%20risk%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract only). NSF guideline page, https://www.thensf.org/sleep-schedules-sleep-timing-guideline/
usable.population: Windred: 60,977 UK Biobank adults, mean age 62.8, 97% white, 1 week of accelerometry. Fang: 2,115 first-year US medical interns. Outcomes are mortality and depression, not burnout.
usable.implication: Track the 14-day spread of wake time and sleep duration and compare it only with the user's own baseline. Do not invent a population cut-off such as a fixed number of minutes. The effect is small in r2 terms, so give it low weight. The Sleep Regularity Index is built from accelerometry; logged bed and wake times are a coarser proxy.
usable.note: Windred: fully adjusted all-cause HR 0.70 (0.59-0.83) top vs bottom regularity quintile; duration 0.76 (0.65-0.89). No optimal cut-off defined; 97.2% white, mean age 62.8, one week of accelerometry. Fang 2021 abstract: n=2,115 interns, b=0.4 and b=0.081, r2 0.01 each, smaller day-to-day shifts linked to better mood. NSF page sets no numeric limit. Sample sizes differ inside Windred: 60,977 in the Abstract, 60,997 in Results, and fully adjusted models used N=46,721. The HR confidence intervals overlap, so 'at least as strongly' fits better than 'stronger'.

usable.claim: Prospective links between short or poor sleep and burnout exist but are small, inconsistent and bidirectional in some studies. Threshold status: the only cut-point, under 6 h, rests on one study with 15 incident cases. I found no meta-analysis pooling prospective sleep-to-burnout effects.
usable.values: Soderstrom: under 6 h was the main risk factor after adjustment; no OR in abstract. Armon: insomnia to new burnout OR 1.64 (1.30-2.08); burnout to new insomnia OR 1.93 (1.45-2.58); beta .05 to .07. Jansson-Frojmark: insomnia did not predict burnout incidence, but predicted persistent emotional exhaustion OR 3.02.
usable.source: Soderstrom M et al. 2012, J Occup Health Psychol (abstract only). Armon G et al. 2008, J Psychosom Res, https://cris.tau.ac.il/en/publications/on-the-nature-of-burnout-insomnia-relationships-a-prospective-stu/ (abstract). Jansson-Frojmark M, Lindblom K 2010, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22Is%20There%20a%20Bidirectional%20Link%20Between%20Insomnia%20and%20Burnout%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract).
usable.population: Working adults: 388 in Sweden over 2 years; 1,356 apparently healthy employed adults over 18 months; 1,258 employed Swedes over 1 year.
usable.implication: Sleep is a reasonable contributor but cannot carry a burnout threshold alone. Under 6 h can be a soft warning, not a burnout rule. Because worsening sleep may be a symptom as well as a cause, the app should describe it as a co-moving signal and not as the reason.
usable.note: Soderstrom 2012 abstract: 388 Swedish workers, 2 years, 15 clinical burnout cases, under 6 h the main risk factor after adjustment, no OR given. Armon abstract: n=1,356, about 18 months, OR 1.64 (1.30-2.08) and 1.93 (1.45-2.58), betas .05 and .07. Jansson-Frojmark 2010 abstract: 1,258 employed analysed, 1 year, no incidence link either way, persistent emotional exhaustion OR 3.02. NOT TESTED: 'no meta-analysis pooling prospective sleep-to-burnout effects' is a negative search claim. The session's WebSearch budget ran out, so this one stands only on the researcher's word.

usable.claim: Cite Pega F et al. 2021 for 745,194 deaths. State follow-up as 1-20 years for incidence and 8-30 years for IHD mortality. Note the stroke 49-54 h rating is 'limited' and the 55+ h stroke mortality rating is 'inadequate'.
usable.values: 55 h or more: stroke incidence RR 1.35 (1.13-1.61); IHD incidence RR 1.13 (1.02-1.26); IHD mortality RR 1.17 (1.05-1.31). 49-54 h: stroke RR 1.13 (1.00-1.28), IHD RR 1.05 (0.94-1.17). 41-48 h: stroke RR 1.04 (0.94-1.14), IHD RR 0.98 (0.91-1.07), rated inadequate. 745,194 attributable deaths in 2016.
usable.source: Descatha A et al. 2020, Environment International (abstract). Li J et al. 2020, Environment International, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22effect%20of%20exposure%20to%20long%20working%20hours%20on%20ischaemic%20heart%20disease%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract). WHO news release, https://www.who.int/news/item/17-05-2021-long-working-hours-increasing-deaths-from-heart-disease-and-stroke-who-ilo
usable.population: Workers in cohort studies across WHO regions, followed 1-20 years. Paid work only, not study or side projects.
usable.implication: For working users, a sustained multi-week average of 55 h or more of load is the strongest evidence-backed upper default. Treat 49-54 h as an amber band. Word it as long-term health risk. Never present it as the burnout line, and never apply it to one week.
usable.note: All RRs match the abstracts: stroke 55+ 1.35 (1.13-1.61), 49-54 1.13 (1.00-1.28), 41-48 1.04 (0.94-1.14); IHD incidence 1.13 (1.02-1.26), mortality 1.17 (1.05-1.31), 49-54 1.05, 41-48 0.98. Defects: (1) 745,194 is in none of the three cited sources. The WHO release says 745,000; the exact figure is Pega et al. 2021, Environ Int 154, which I confirmed in Europe PMC (UI 705,786-784,601). (2) '1-20 years' fits the 55+ incidence estimates, but IHD mortality follow-up is 8-30 years. (3) Ratings differ by band: stroke 49-54 h is 'limited', not inadequate. At 55+ h, stroke mortality (RR 1.08, 0.89-1.31) and IHD prevalence are 'inadequate', so 'sufficient' covers only the three outcomes listed.

usable.claim: Korea: direct-effect ORs 1.18 (1.05-1.33) and 1.20 (1.04-1.37), with additional indirect effects via work-family conflict (n=19,159). Rugulies 55+ h: 17 studies, 91,142 people. Lin: spline-based, work-related burnout subscale, reference 40 h or less.
usable.values: Rugulies, 55 h or more: OR 1.08 (0.94-1.24), rated inadequate evidence. Virtanen: OR 1.14 (1.03-1.25); Asia 1.50 (1.13-2.01), Europe 1.11, North America 0.97, Australia 0.95. Lin: 41-59 h OR 1.50, 60 h or more OR 1.90; odds about 2x near 60 h, 3x near 74 h, 4x near 84 h. Korea: 49-54 h OR 1.18 (1.05-1.33), 55 h or more OR 1.20 (1.04-1.37).
usable.source: Rugulies R et al. 2021, Environment International (abstract). Virtanen M et al. 2018, Scand J Work Environ Health, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:29423526%20AND%20SRC:MED&format=json&resultType=core (abstract). Lin RT et al. 2021, J Occup Health, https://academic.oup.com/joh/article/63/1/e12228/7249820 (first 100,000 characters read). Korean KWCS analysis, BJPsych Open 2023, PMID 37670723, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=(TITLE:%22long%20working%20hours%22%20AND%20TITLE:burnout%20AND%20(korea%20OR%20korean))&format=json&resultType=core (abstract).
usable.population: Rugulies: 22 cohorts, 109,906 workers. Virtanen: 189,729 workers in 35 countries. Lin: 2,081 Taiwanese health care workers, cross-sectional. KWCS: Korean workers, cross-sectional.
usable.implication: Default to a gentle slope above about 48 h with no hard burnout line, then learn each person's sensitivity. The stronger Asian estimate suggests a slightly steeper Korean default, but that is hypothesis, not proof.
usable.note: Confirmed: Rugulies OR 1.08 (0.94-1.24), inadequate evidence, first author Rugulies per Europe PMC (the CDC page lists authors alphabetically, Ahn first). Virtanen numbers all match. Lin 41-59 h 1.50 and 60+ h 1.90 against 40 h or less. Defects: (1) Korean ORs 1.18 and 1.20 are direct effects from a mediation model, not total effects; indirect effects via work-family conflict are OR 1.11 and 1.20 (Baek, Won, Yoon 2023, n=19,159). The abstract gives no reference category and does not state the design outright. (2) 109,906 workers is the total across all 22 studies; the 55+ h estimate uses 17 studies and 91,142 people. (3) Lin's 2x/3x/4x points come from the fitted spline for the work-related burnout subscale only; Results give about 59, 73 and 84 h at 1-month averages, and the categorical 60+ h OR is below 2. NOT TESTED: 'no dose-response meta-analysis of hours and burnout' is a negative search claim and the search budget ran out.

usable.claim: Workload has the largest pooled estimate among predictors with at least 3 studies, but not overall. The 'no change across 3-48 months' finding belongs to the job demands subfamily, not workload specifically.
usable.values: Workload rho 0.38 (0.34-0.43; 6 studies), about 14% shared variance by my calculation. Time pressure 0.35. Job demands 0.33, range 0.33-0.39 across 3-48 months. Sleep and physical activity were not analysed as predictors.
usable.source: Shoman Y, Rousson V, Bianchi R, Guseva Canu I 2022, Int J Environ Res Public Health (first 100,000 of 168,000 characters read).
usable.population: 65 longitudinal studies, 242 predictors, mean age 31, about 75% women, mostly European workers.
usable.implication: Give load the largest default weight, and show that population data explain only a minority of risk. This supports the owner's plan for a personal layer. The persistent association over months supports windows of weeks, not days.
usable.note: Numbers match: rho 0.38 (0.34-0.43, k=6), time pressure 0.35, job demands 0.33; 65 studies, 242 predictors, mean age 31, 75% women, 47 of 65 European. Job demands cumulative rho runs 0.33-0.39 over 3-48 months and is labelled no change. Sleep and physical activity absent from Table 1. Two defects: (1) Workload is not the strongest pooled predictor. Table 1 shows psychological/physical toll 0.44 (k=2) and flow -0.40 (k=1), and reward reaches -0.42 after dropping one study. Workload is highest in the job demands family and among Table 1 entries with k of 3 or more. (2) The time analysis was run on subfamilies only; workload itself was not analysed over time.

usable.claim: Say: the 40 + 12 rule implies 52 h/week as the ordinary limit, subject to flexible-hours schemes, special extended work and Art. 59 exceptions. The notice covers cerebrovascular, heart and musculoskeletal disease. Treat all legal wording as third-party until checked against law.go.kr.
usable.values: Statute: 40 h/week and 8 h/day, plus up to 12 h overtime by agreement, so 52 h/week; a week is 7 days including holidays. Notice: 12-week average over 60 h (or 4-week average over 64 h) means strong association; over 52 h, association rises with hours; under 52 h can count with multiple burdens. Acute rule: last-week hours or workload up 30% or more against the prior 12-week average. Night work 22:00-06:00 counts 1.3x.
usable.source: Ministry of Employment and Labor Notice 2026-14, issued 23 Feb 2026 per a third-party full-text reproduction. Labor Standards Act articles via third-party summary, https://korea.legal/wiki/%EC%97%B0%EC%9E%A5%EA%B7%BC%EB%A1%9C%EC%9D%98-%ED%95%9C%EB%8F%84%EC%99%80-%EA%B0%80%EC%82%B0%EC%9E%84%EA%B8%88/. The official law.go.kr page did not render, so official wording is unverified.
usable.population: Employees in Korea. Articles 50 and 53 apply to workplaces with 5 or more workers. Not students; self-employed people are outside the Act's employee framing.
usable.implication: Reasonable Korean defaults: 52 h amber, 60 h (12-week) or 64 h (4-week) red. The +30% against own 12-week average rule is directly implementable as a personal spike trigger. Label it as a Korean administrative benchmark, and do not apply it to students as if it were law. Confirm wording on the official site before shipping.
usable.note: LEGAL CAUTION. Only third-party text was seen. law.go.kr returned titles only, and I could not open an official copy, so official wording stays unverified. The korea.legal page gives issue and effective date 23 Feb 2026, links no official source, says the official text controls, and never states it is the complete notice. Matching that page: 12-week average over 60 h (or 4-week over 64 h) strong link; over 52 h rising link; under 52 h with multiple burdens; last week up 30% or more vs prior 12-week average (excluding that week); night work 22:00 to 06:00 with a 30% add-on, breaks excluded, with an exception for approved supervised or intermittent work. Defects: (1) the notice also covers musculoskeletal disease. (2) '52 h/week' is arithmetic: the statute page states 40 + 12 and no general ceiling, and it describes flexible schedules, special extended work with ministerial approval (Art. 53(4)) and Art. 59 exceptions that can exceed it. (3) The 'week includes holidays' definition phased in by workplace size from 2018 to 2021.

usable.claim: Say 'health care was the largest sector (10 of 22 studies)' and give the moderate-bias vs all-study split for weekly hours.
usable.values: Over 12 h/day vs 8 h or less: RR 1.24 (1.11-1.40) in moderate-bias studies; RR 1.24 (0.85-1.81) across all eight studies. 41-48 and 49-54 h/week: RR about 1.02, null. GRADE low or very low. EU: 11 consecutive hours daily rest, 24 h weekly rest plus the 11, 48 h average week.
usable.source: Matre D et al. 2021, safety incidents meta-analysis, Scand J Work Environ Health (first 100,000 of 110,000 characters read). EU Directive 2003/88/EC Articles 3, 5, 6, 16 via an unofficial Wikisource copy, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/European_Working_Time_Directive. EUR-Lex did not render.
usable.population: 22 studies, mostly health care workers; outcome is incidents, not burnout. EU rules apply to EU workers.
usable.implication: Do not fire a burnout alert from one long day. Aggregate daily minutes into rolling weekly load. If a marker is wanted, use a neutral long-day note at 12 h, and optionally note when the gap between days falls under 11 h, labelled as a legal convention.
usable.note: Matre 2021: 22 studies; over 12 h/day RR 1.24 (0.85-1.81) in eight studies, 1.24 (1.11-1.40) in three moderate-bias studies; GRADE low or very low. The RR of about 1.02 for 41-48 and 49-54 h is the moderate-bias subset; all-study values are 1.15 (0.95-1.39) and 1.09 (0.90-1.32), also null. The paper says most studies concern health care, but Table 1 shows 10 of 22, the largest group rather than a majority. EU rules checked on Wikisource only, as EUR-Lex returned empty for me too: 11 h daily, 24 h plus 11 h weekly, 48 h average including overtime. Art. 16 allows reference periods up to 14 days for weekly rest and 4 months for the 48 h; Art. 5 allows a 24 h minimum where justified.

usable.claim: Study hours have no established burnout threshold, and worker cut-offs should not be transferred to students. PISA 2015 found no significant average relationship between study time and life satisfaction. In Korean adolescents, the clearer signal is very short sleep. Threshold status: none for study hours; under 5 h sleep is an association band, not a threshold.
usable.values: PISA: no significant relationship for study time in or out of school; test frequency unrelated to schoolwork anxiety. KYRBS, under 5 h vs 7 to under 9 h: depressive symptoms aOR 1.40 male, 1.38 female; suicidal ideation aOR 1.65 male, 1.58 female.
usable.source: OECD 2017, PISA 2015 Results Volume III Overview (overview document read, not the full volume). Korean KYRBS analysis, Sci Rep 2022, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC9205903/fullTextXML (first 100,000 characters read).
usable.population: 15-year-olds across PISA countries (outcome is life satisfaction, not burnout). 270,619 Korean students in grades 7-12, 2015-2019.
usable.implication: For students, set no population study-hour limit. Start from the person's own baseline and let the model learn. Weight sleep more than hours by default. Because suicidal ideation correlates with very short sleep, warnings for teens need supportive wording and a pointer to real help, not a score.
usable.note: The PDF text states no significant average relationship between time spent studying, in or out of school, and life satisfaction, and that test frequency is unrelated to schoolwork-related anxiety. That test frequency is principal-reported. KYRBS (Lee et al. 2022, Sci Rep): n=270,619, grades 7-12, 2015-2019, reference 7 to under 9 h; under 5 h depressive symptoms aOR 1.40 male, 1.38 female; suicidal ideation 1.65 male, 1.58 female. 'Worker cut-offs should not be transferred to students' is the researcher's judgement, not a source finding.

usable.claim: Population: daily non-work time (afternoon and evening), not evening only; weekend and vacation detachment excluded.
usable.values: Detachment with exhaustion r=-0.36 (k=23), fatigue r=-0.42 (k=17), sleep r=0.30 (k=18), job demands r=-0.25. Lagged exhaustion k=4 r=-0.34. I2 85-98%. Fatigue prediction interval -0.78 to 0.17, so a new setting could show the opposite.
usable.source: Wendsche J, Lohmann-Haislah A 2017, Frontiers in Psychology (first 100,000 of 224,000 characters read). Bennett AA et al. 2018, J Organ Behav, https://pure.uj.ac.za/en/publications/recovery-from-work-related-effort-a-meta-analysis/ (abstract). Geurts SAE, Sonnentag S 2006, https://www.sjweh.fi/article/1053 (abstract; theoretical paper).
usable.population: Employees: 91 samples, N=38,124, mean age 39.9, mostly European, evening detachment only. Bennett: 54 samples, N=26,592. Students not covered.
usable.implication: Recovery should not equal exercise minutes alone. Add one optional daily self-worded item on whether the user switched off from work or study. Keep this scored within person, since no cut-off exists. Do not copy Recovery Experience Questionnaire items.
usable.note: Numbers match Wendsche 2017: k=91, N=38,124, mean age 39.9, exhaustion r=-.36 (k=23), fatigue r=-.42 (k=17), sleep r=.30 (k=18), job demands r=-.25, lagged exhaustion k=4 r=-.34, fatigue prediction interval -.78 to .17. I2 for the listed outcomes is 85.76, 97.86, 94.55 and 89.34, so 85-98% holds for those, though the full table runs from about 13% to 98%. Bennett and Geurts abstracts match. Defect: 'evening detachment only' is wrong. The authors cover daily non-work time, afternoon and evening, excluding intervals longer than a day and during-work periods. The k=4 subgroup is flagged for caution.

usable.claim: Say 'studied range 4-23 days', not 'vacations over 3 weeks unstudied'.
usable.values: Overall well-being d=0.25; positive affect, negative affect, stress and exhaustion ds 0.18-0.38. No significant difference from pre-vacation by the first post-vacation week (ds 0.12 or lower). De Bloom: d=+0.43 then fade-out d=-0.38.
usable.source: Speth F, Wendsche J, Wegge J 2023, European Psychologist (abstract only). De Bloom J et al. 2009, J Occup Health, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/joh/51/1/51_K8004/_article (abstract only).
usable.population: Employees: 13 studies, N=1,428, mean vacation 11 days, range 4-23. Few studies; vacations over 3 weeks unstudied.
usable.implication: A holiday must not reset accumulated load in the model. Give recovery credit a short half-life of days, and favour steady weekly recovery over rare long breaks. Half-life values remain a design assumption to refine per person.
usable.note: Speth 2023 abstract: 13 studies, N=1,428, mean about 11 days, range 4-23, overall d=0.25, facets 0.18-0.38, duration did not moderate, no significant difference by the end of the first post-vacation week (d 0.12 or lower). De Bloom 2009: d=+0.43, fade-out d=-0.38. Slip: the range reaches 23 days, slightly past 3 weeks, so 'over 3 weeks unstudied' is loose.

usable.claim: Weekend rebound differs between people, and limited rebound may mark burnout. What happens at the weekend matters, not only hours off. Threshold status: no evidence found for a required number of rest days. One in seven is a legal floor, not a recovery dose.
usable.values: Three morning and three evening fatigue trajectory classes, differing in weekday level and weekend recovery. Non-work hassles, no positive work reflection and low social activity at the weekend predicted burnout and poorer well-being afterwards.
usable.source: Gatari E, Fleuren BPI, Zijlstra FRH, Hulsheger UR 2025, J Occup Health Psychol (abstract only). Fritz C, Sonnentag S 2005, J Occup Health Psychol, https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/bitstream/123456789/11226/1/Recovery_health_and_job_performance.pdf (abstract and introduction read).
usable.population: 297 employees over 16 diary days; 87 emergency service workers over 3 measurements. Short windows; no burnout incidence.
usable.implication: Compute a weekly rebound score: energy after rest days minus energy before them, against the user's norm. Several weeks of poor rebound is a candidate personal signal, unvalidated as a predictor. Morning and evening fatigue behaved differently, so an optional second daily energy rating could add value.
usable.note: Gatari 2025: 297 employees, 16 diary days, three morning and three evening fatigue classes differing in weekday level and weekend recovery; limited weekend recovery could reflect burnout. Fritz and Sonnentag 2005 abstract: 87 emergency service workers, 3 measurements, non-work hassles, absence of positive work reflection and low social activity predicted burnout and poor well-being after the weekend. The predictors come from Fritz only; the Gatari page does not name them. 'One in seven is a legal floor' has no source cited here and was not checked.

usable.claim: Say 'some remain unrecovered 7-12 years later' instead of 'never'. Give denominators: 163 for clinical figures, 217 for self-report.
usable.values: Dutch cohort: 37% full return to work at 6 months; poor sleep benefit predicted worse exhaustion. Glise at about 7 years: 31% of 163 assessed still clinically exhausted, 61% no longer met criteria, 16% self-rated fully recovered, 73% reduced stress tolerance, 42% memory problems. 10 years: 28% of working participants at or above the 4.4 cut-off, 31.5% had reduced hours.
usable.source: Glise K, Wiegner L, Jonsdottir IH 2020, BMC Psychology (full text). Sonnenschein M et al. 2008, Scand J Work Environ Health, https://www.sjweh.fi/article/1195 (abstract). 10-year Umea follow-up, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11267866/ (full text).
usable.population: 217 Swedish exhaustion-disorder patients (74% women, 65% response); 59 Dutch burnt-out employees on extended sick leave; 107 Swedish rehabilitation patients (50% response). Severe, selected cases.
usable.implication: After a user marks an episode, keep an open recovery state rather than auto-clearing it. Do not merge pre- and post-episode baselines, because tolerance may be lower afterwards. Separate clinical severity from everyday overload in wording, and do not promise a date.
usable.note: Glise 2020: 217 of 334 responded (65%), 74% women. 31% and 61% are of 163 clinically assessed, 7-12 years after initial care rather than exactly 7. 16%, 73% and 42% are of the 217 questionnaire responders. The memory figure is 42% in Table 3 but 43% in the text. Sonnenschein 2008 abstract: n=59, 37% full return to work, poor sleep benefit linked to higher exhaustion. Umea 10-year: 107, 50% response, 25 of 89 working at or above 4.4 on the SMBQ, 28 of 88 reduced hours. 'Never fully recover' goes beyond the data, which show non-recovery at up to about 10-12 years.

usable.claim: Replace 'sets no minimum' with 'says benefits accrue from any amount'. Add that most Singh reviews were critically low quality.
usable.values: Adults 18-64: 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 min vigorous per week, plus strength on 2 or more days. Ages 5-17: average 60 min/day. Pearce: half the recommended volume 18% lower depression risk (13-23%), recommended volume 25% (18-32%). Singh: depression -0.43, anxiety -0.42, distress -0.60; higher intensity better; effects smaller in longer interventions.
usable.source: Bull FC et al. 2020, WHO guidelines, Br J Sports Med (first 100,000 of 114,000 characters read). Pearce M et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:35416941%20AND%20SRC:MED&format=json&resultType=core (abstract). Singh B et al. 2023, Br J Sports Med, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22Effectiveness%20of%20physical%20activity%20interventions%20for%20improving%20depression%2C%20anxiety%20and%20distress%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract).
usable.population: WHO: general population by age. Pearce: 15 studies, 191,130 adults, incident depression. Singh: 97 reviews, 1,039 trials, 128,119 people. Outcomes are health, depression and distress, not burnout.
usable.implication: Score recovery activity on a concave curve: most credit in the first 75 minutes per week, tapering by 150-300 minutes for adults, with 60 min/day as the target for under 18. Show no failure state below target. The app does not record intensity, so minutes alone understate or overstate the dose.
usable.note: Bull 2020: 150-300 min moderate or 75-150 vigorous, strength on 2+ days, ages 5-17 average 60 min/day, curvilinear dose-response, gains diminish at higher levels. WHO does not literally say 'no minimum'; it says some activity is better than none and benefits accrue from any amount, and that the point of diminishing returns cannot be specified. Pearce: 15 studies, 191,130 adults, 18% (13-23) and 25% (18-32), compared with inactive adults, I2 74%. Singh: 97 reviews, 1,039 trials, 128,119 people; -0.43 and -0.42 are median effect sizes; 77 of 97 reviews rated critically low on AMSTAR, a caveat the claim omits.

usable.claim: Drop Wang's overall SMDs as exercise evidence, or label them as mostly mindfulness trials. State Ochentel pooled 4 RCTs, n=248.
usable.values: Ochentel pooled 95% CI -0.41 to 0.09, no clear difference. Naczenski: exhaustion favoured, only one high-quality study. De Vries, 6 weeks, 3 sessions weekly at low intensity: fatigue eta2=.05, need for recovery .08, sleep quality .09, emotional exhaustion .01 not significant. Wang: overall SMD -0.33 in Results, -0.45 in Abstract; exhaustion -0.05 not significant; review has internal inconsistencies.
usable.source: Ochentel O, Humphrey C, Pfeifer K 2018, J Sports Sci Med (full text). Naczenski LM et al. 2017, J Occup Health, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC5721270/fullTextXML (full text). De Vries JD et al. 2016, PLoS One, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4816334/fullTextXML (full text). Wang W, Zhang P 2026, Frontiers in Psychology, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1840246/full
usable.population: Ochentel: 6 RCTs in people with burnout. Naczenski: 10 studies of employees. De Vries: 100 fatigued Dutch university students. Wang: students, 5 burnout trials, n=610.
usable.implication: Give exercise a modest default buffer and let the personal model estimate it. Never present exercise as a burnout treatment, and avoid prompting an exhausted user to do more. For students, the honest message is that it may ease fatigue and improve sleep quality.
usable.note: Ochentel: CI -0.41 to 0.09 confirmed, dose about 2-3 sessions per week of 30-60 min, but only 4 of the 6 RCTs (n=248) were pooled. Naczenski: 10 studies, 1 high quality; its authors nonetheless conclude activity is effective. De Vries: eta2 .05, .08, .09, .01 ns confirmed. Wang: -0.45 in Abstract, -0.33 in Results, exhaustion -0.05 ns, 5 trials, n=610 confirmed. Main defect: per Wang's Table 1, 4 of the 5 burnout trials are mindfulness (Xin, Kewei, Oro, de Vibe) and only Fisher 2016 is aerobic exercise. Those SMDs therefore are not exercise effects and should not be evidence on exercise and burnout. The review's own eligibility rules conflict with that classification.

usable.claim: Say: in full models reactivity remained associated with distress and self-reported disorder while frequency did not; no formal comparison was run, and reactivity did not predict symptom-based diagnosis.
usable.values: Distress at 10 years: negative affect on non-stressor days beta=.18, reactivity beta=.13, stressor frequency beta=.02 not significant. Self-reported disorder: reactivity OR 1.56 (1.21-2.01), frequency OR 1.10 not significant in full model. Leger reports no numeric effect in the abstract.
usable.source: Charles ST et al. 2013, Psychological Science (full text). Leger KA, Charles ST, Almeida DM 2018, Psychological Science, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:29993345%20OR%20TITLE:%22Let%20it%20go%3A%20lingering%20negative%20affect%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract only).
usable.population: US community adults aged 25-74, 711 and 1,155 people, 94% European American in Charles. 8 diary days, 10-year outcomes of distress, affective disorder and physical health, not burnout.
usable.implication: Do not sum stress ratings alone. Compute personal features: mood on low-stress days, mood drop per stress point, and next-day carryover. These need many days before they stabilise. Accumulation itself remains less proven than reactivity, so the stock model should be presented as a working estimate.
usable.note: Numbers match Charles 2013: distress beta .18, .13, .02 ns; disorder reactivity OR 1.56 (1.21-2.01), frequency 1.10 (0.83-1.45) ns; n=711, 94% European American. Leger 2018: n=1,155, 8 days, physical health about 10 years later, no effect sizes in the abstract. Overreach: the paper never formally compares reactivity with frequency, which entered as a covariate.
