Reactivity was not significant for symptom-based diagnosis in the full model (OR 1.25, 0.92-1.70). Frequency was significant in Model 1 for self-reported disorder (OR 1.30, 1.02-1.66). Physical health is an outcome only in Leger.

usable.claim: Name the authors: Basinska BA, Gruszczynska E 2020; the sample is Polish.
usable.values: ICC exhaustion 0.41, disengagement 0.45, so about 59% and 55% within person. Same-day residual correlations 0.64-0.76. Only 7 of 18 autoregressive paths significant. Repeated lag: Monday disengagement to Tuesday exhaustion beta=.22 and .21.
usable.source: Burnout as a State: random-intercept cross-lagged study of exhaustion and disengagement, Psychology Research and Behavior Management (full text).
usable.population: 235 public-sector civil servants, about 75% women, 10 consecutive workdays. No onset data.
usable.implication: Score each day against the user's own mean and spread, not the 1-5 scale midpoint. Require a multi-day pattern before any alert, since one bad day predicts little. Weekday effects suggest comparing like days in the baseline.
usable.note: Basinska and Gruszczynska 2020 (PRBM 13:267-278): 235 Polish civil servants, 75% women, 10 workdays; ICC 0.41 and 0.45; same-day residual correlations 0.64-0.76; 7 of 18 autoregressive paths significant; Monday disengagement to Tuesday exhaustion .22 and .21. Within-person shares (59%, 55%) are correct arithmetic from the ICCs. 'Situation more than a smooth build-up' and 'supports personal baselines' are the researcher's inferences.

usable.claim: Maunz stressors to burnout: -.04 to .01. Hadzibajramovic: reward only (low and medium levels), single 2-year lag.
usable.values: Maunz, within person per 6 months: burnout to overload beta .07-.11, social stressors .12-.15, organizational stressors .08-.12; stressors to burnout about .00 to -.04. Stressors did raise burnout for people with chronically low resources or high stressors. Sorjonen: 23 reported effects, nearly all did not withstand scrutiny. Hadzibajramovic: at a 2-year lag only low reward remained.
usable.source: Guthier C, Dormann C, Voelkle MC 2020, Psychological Bulletin (abstract only). Maunz LA et al. 2026, J Occup Health Psychol, https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2026-99528-001.pdf (abstract and selected results read). Sorjonen K et al. 2025, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1618120/pdf (abstract read). Hadzibajramovic E et al. 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6768907/ (full text). Dormann C, Griffin MA 2015, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22Optimal%20time%20lags%20in%20panel%20studies%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract).
usable.population: Guthier: 48 studies, N=26,319 employees, few with intervals under 12 months. Maunz: 2,131 German-speaking employees, 5 waves over 24 months. Hadzibajramovic: 3,209 Swedish health care staff.
usable.implication: Do not hard-code a lag such as N weeks of high stress. Rising stress may be an early symptom, so report co-movement and avoid causal language. Personal thresholds should be learned as association from the user's own episodes and stay labelled as an estimate.
usable.note: Guthier abstract: k=48, N=26,319, stressor-to-burnout small, reverse larger, few intervals under 12 months, no numeric values in the abstract. Maunz 2026 (JOHP 31(1):42-62), PDF text read: 2,131 employees, 5 waves, 24 months; .07-.11, .12-.15, .08-.12 confirmed; conditional effect for low resources or high stressors confirmed. Sorjonen 2025: 23 effects, all but possibly one did not hold up; these are simulated reanalyses, not original data. Dormann 2015 supports short optimal lags. Small fixes: reverse-path betas run -.04 to +.01 (social stressors .01). Hadzibajramovic Table 4 also shows medium reward significant, and only a 2-year lag was tested.

usable.claim: Under extreme sustained load, burnout can rise sharply within a year, which sets a months-long timescale for accumulation. Threshold status: descriptive prevalence change from one small cohort; no time-to-onset was measured.
usable.values: High burnout 4.3% to 55.3%. High chronic sleep deprivation 9% to 43%. Moderate depression 4.3% to 29.8%. Becoming chronically sleep deprived linked to becoming depressed, OR 7.
usable.source: Rosen IM et al. 2006, Academic Medicine (abstract only).
usable.population: 47 internal medicine interns at one US program, 2002-03, measured at start and end of year. Not generalisable.
usable.implication: Accumulation windows should span weeks to months, and one user may log few or no burnout events a year. Personal thresholds therefore cannot rely on full episodes alone. Collect milder events such as a periodic self-check or a user-marked near miss, and keep the population prior for a long time.
usable.note: Rosen 2006 abstract: 47 interns, University of Pennsylvania, 2002-03, burnout 4.3% to 55.3%, chronic sleep deprivation 9% to 43%, moderate depression 4.3% to 29.8%, OR 7 (p=.014). Measured only at start and year end, so the 'months-long timescale' is an inference from two time points.

usable.claim: Stages run enthusiasm, weakening ideal, protective withdrawal with cynicism, confirmed burnout. Workers are usually unaware before Stage 3, though first signs may appear at Stages 1-2.
usable.values: No stage durations given; burnout typically recognised only at the last stage. Diary: 8,116 entries; burned-out participants showed continuous severe fatigue with flattened diurnal cycles.
usable.source: Temporal Stages of Burnout: How to Design Prevention? (narrative opinion review, first 100,000 of 197,000 characters read). Sonnenschein M et al. 2007, J Occup Health Psychol, https://www.wilmarschaufeli.nl/publications/Schaufeli/284.pdf (abstract read).
usable.population: Stage model rests on nine qualitative or descriptive studies. Diary study: 60 clinically burned-out and 40 healthy Dutch adults, 14 days, 7 entries a day.
usable.implication: Treat low energy persistence, loss of rebound and growing disengagement as hypotheses to test per user, not as a validated checklist. A flat signal needs at least two ratings a day. The current index mostly captures exhaustion, so a separate cynicism or disengagement item is needed to see the wider construct.
usable.note: Leclercq and Hansez 2024 (IJERPH 21(12):1617), opinion review; nine qualitative and descriptive studies confirmed. I read both halves of the 197,000-character text and found no durations for stages 0-3. Sonnenschein 2007 abstract confirmed: 60 clinical and 40 healthy, 14 days, 7 times daily, 8,116 entries, flattened cycles. Defects: stages are framed as weakening ideals and protective withdrawal, not declining energy; energy loss appears in the general symptom description, and Stage 0 has high energy. Also, the source says the worker is usually unaware before Stage 3, yet it places first clinical signs at Stages 1-2. So the point concerns the worker's awareness, not recognition in general. The diary sample was on extended sick leave.

usable.claim: State Helmich concerns improvement transitions in therapy. Add that Smit found variance trends differed by recurrence, though sensitivity was low.
usable.values: Rising autocorrelation in at least one variable: 89% with a transition vs 62.5% without. Rising variance: about 11% vs 12%. In tapering sample, signals preceded recurrence in 32.9% across robustness checks.
usable.source: Helmich MA et al. 2021 and Smit AC et al. 2022, PsyArXiv preprints, abstracts only. The published journal page was blocked (HTTP 403). Reading the percentages as detections and false flags is my interpretation.
usable.population: 41 depressed people starting treatment; 37 formerly depressed people tapering antidepressants. Dutch clinical samples, not burnout.
usable.implication: Do not ship variance or autocorrelation alarms on one 1-5 rating a day. Use simple, explainable pattern rules against personal baseline, phrased as something worth noticing. If tested later, measure false alarm rate on the user's own history first.
usable.note: Numbers match the preprint abstracts: 89% vs 62.5%, about 11% vs 12%, 32.9%, n=41 and n=37, five times daily for 4 months. Defects: (1) Helmich's transitions are toward lower symptoms during therapy, so 'no transition' means no improvement, not no relapse. Transferring this to burnout onset is a further step. (2) The claim omits that in Smit the recurrence group had significantly more positive variance trends and over three times as many signals, which conflicts with using Helmich's flat variance result alone. Both are preprints and group sizes are not given. The abstracts do not state the country; Groningen appears only in the protocol. The headline fits the authors' low-sensitivity and limited-value conclusions but is the researcher's inference.

usable.claim: Name the authors: Garcia JC, Arteaga A 2024.
usable.values: No two studies used the same marker combination; about 70% reported an association; 3 of 5 MBI studies linked to allostatic load. Danhof-Pont meta-analyses found no differences for cortisol awakening response, blood cortisol or blood pressure.
usable.source: Allostatic load and physiological responses to work stress: an integrative review (full text). Danhof-Pont MB, van Veen T, Zitman FG 2011, J Psychosom Res, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=TITLE:%22Biomarkers%20in%20burnout%3A%20a%20systematic%20review%22&format=json&resultType=core (abstract).
usable.population: 17 work-stress studies, 15 cross-sectional, sample sizes 30 to over 8,000. Danhof-Pont: 31 studies of 38 biomarkers.
usable.implication: Use the idea only as a plain metaphor for wear from repeated strain. Do not call a self-report stock allostatic load, and do not imply a physiological measurement. A neutral name such as accumulated strain estimate is safer and more honest.
usable.note: Garcia and Arteaga 2024 (Rev Bras Med Trab): 17 studies, 15 cross-sectional, 2 longitudinal, n=30 to 8,028, no identical marker combinations, 70% reported an association, 3 of 5 MBI studies linked; the MBI subscales and versions vary. Danhof-Pont 2011 abstract: 31 studies, 38 biomarkers, no differences for CAR, CAR after dexamethasone, blood cortisol or blood pressure, no potential biomarker found, mainly due to incomparable studies. That biomarker review is from 2011, so 'no accepted biomarker' rests on older evidence.

usable.claim: Two small limits. 'Equivalent' means all p > .05; the paper names no formal equivalence test. Sample 2's duration is not stated (mean 925 observations per person), so '6 to 100 days' covers only the samples that give a duration.
usable.values: Within-person SD was 3.79 to 13.20 times the between-person SD across 15 variables (mean 7.85). Means equivalent for 14 of 15 variables. Only about 68% of individual correlations fell in the range group data predicted would hold 99.7%.
usable.source: Fisher AJ, Medaglia JD, Jeronimus BF (2018). Lack of group-to-individual generalizability is a threat to human subjects research. PNAS 115(27):E6106-E6115.
usable.population: Six US and Dutch clinical and community repeated-measures samples, 6 to 100 days. Mood, anxiety and heart measures, not burnout.
usable.implication: Population numbers can seed a person's mean, but not their spread or which variables move together. Estimate each person's SD from their own data, and do not ship fixed population z-cutoffs as personal limits.
usable.note: Full text read. Confirmed: SD ratio 3.79:1 to 13.20:1 (mean 7.85) across 15 variables, means equivalent on 14 of 15, about 68% of individual correlations inside the group-predicted 99.7% range, and no agreement between variances. Six US and Dutch samples. Authors, year and citation match.

usable.claim: 59 to 70% is the item-level range. At scale level, within-person variance is 59% for exhaustion and 55% for disengagement. The scale ICCs and the 7 of 18 count appear only in the 2020 paper, which also calls this 'about one-third' in its Discussion.
usable.values: ICC .41 exhaustion and .45 disengagement at scale level, .28 to .41 at item level. Within-person variance 59 to 70%. Only 7 of 18 autoregressive paths were significant. Exhaustion and disengagement correlated .94 within person, .90 between.
usable.source: Gruszczynska E, Basinska BA, Schaufeli WB (2021). PLoS One, multilevel CFA of the OLBI diary. Also Basinska BA, Gruszczynska E (2020). Burnout as a State. Psychol Res Behav Manag 13:267-278, https://www.dovepress.com/burnout-as-a-state-random-intercept-cross-lagged-relationship-between--peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-PRBM
usable.population: 235 white-collar civil servants, 73 to 75% women, 10 consecutive workdays. Poland (inferred from ethics approval and funding).
usable.implication: One day's rating is mostly noise around a person's level, so never flag on a single day. My Spearman-Brown calculation from ICC .28 to .45 gives 5 to 10 daily entries for reliability .80 of the personal mean and 11 to 23 for .90. That ignores autocorrelation, so treat it as a lower bound. Ten days cannot show slow accumulation, so weak carryover does not rule it out.
usable.note: Both papers read. Gruszczynska 2021 gives item ICCs .28 to .41, within-person variance 59 to 70%, and correlations .94 and .90. Basinska and Gruszczynska 2020 gives scale ICCs .41 and .45 and 7 of 18 autoregressive paths significant, and calls the sample white-collar public administration employees. Women 73% and 75%. Poland is inferred, as stated: from affiliations, ethics approval, funder and the Polish OLBI version.

usable.claim: A stable personal mean needs far fewer assessments than stable personal variability, and within-person reliability of affect is only modest.
usable.values: Mean stabilized at about 4 and clearly by about 12 assessments. About 25 were needed for variability. Within-person reliability .48 positive and .59 negative affect, between-person .99. Mean compliance 76.9%, falling across the 15 days.
usable.source: Portillo-Van Diest A, Mortier P, Ballester L, et al. (2024). Ecological Momentary Assessment of Mental Health Problems Among University Students: Data Quality Evaluation Study. J Med Internet Res.
usable.population: 782 Spanish undergraduates, 4 random momentary prompts a day on 14 days. Momentary prompts are not daily summaries, so counts may not carry over one to one.
usable.implication: Stage the app. Show a personal average after about 7 entries, and use personal spread-based flags only after about 25 to 28 entries. By the standard formula the SD estimate has a relative error of about 20% at 14 days, 14% at 28 and 9% at 60. No source gave a day count for one daily rating, so these day numbers are extrapolation.
usable.note: Full text read. 782 undergraduates at 5 public Spanish universities; 4 prompts a day on days 2 to 15; compliance 76.9% with a steady decline; within-person reliability .48 and .59; between-person .99. The mean reached ICC .9 at about 4 assessments and clearly stabilized at about 12; variability needed about 25. These counts are for positive and negative affect, judged against a 40-assessment gold standard.

usable.claim: Shrout pages are E15-E23, not 15-23. Anvari's abstract reports elevation for negative experiences (mood, mental and physical health symptoms). Drop 'though not for trait measures' unless the full text is read.
usable.values: Within-person day 1 vs day 8: d = .47 morning anxious mood, .39 physical symptoms. Median effects .16 to .34 across studies 1 to 3. No decay curve was reported; the elevation sits mainly in the first report.
usable.source: Shrout PE, et al. (2018). Initial elevation bias in subjective reports. PNAS 115(1):15-23. Replication: Anvari F, et al. (2023), Social Psychological and Personality Science 14(6):727-737, https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/bias-in-self-reports-an-initial-elevation-phenomenon/ (abstract only).
usable.population: US law graduates and partners, premed students, undergraduates (four field studies), plus 5,285 Prolific participants in Anvari.
usable.implication: Exclude or down-weight the first 1 to 3 entries from the baseline. As a precedent, a 25-day daily diary (Mak and Schneider 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9071437) discarded its first 4 days as training. My inference: people may also install the app during a bad stretch, so the first baseline should stay provisional and be re-estimated.
usable.note: Shrout figures confirmed in full text: d = .47 morning anxious mood, d = .39 physical symptoms (an evening report), per-study medians .26, .34 and .16, no decay curve fitted, elevation mainly in the first report. Samples match; the US location is implied, not stated outright. Anvari's 5,285 Prolific participants and 'negative subjective experiences' are confirmed. The trait-measures clause is not confirmed: the Maastricht page and the Crossref abstract do not mention traits, and Sage returned 403.

usable.claim: Treating 1 to 5 ratings as metric can produce false alarms, misses and even reversed effects, and averaging several ordinal items does not fix it.
usable.values: 100% of surveyed articles analyzing ordinal data used a metric model. The authors advocate ordered-probit or similar models.
usable.source: Liddell TM, Kruschke JK (2018). Analyzing ordinal data with metric models: What could possibly go wrong? J Exp Soc Psychol 79:328-348. Abstract read on the Indiana University workshop flyer; the article itself was not opened.
usable.population: Methods paper: demonstrations plus a survey of three psychology journals. Not diary data and not one person.
usable.implication: Averages are fine for display but risky as the basis for thresholds. A light alternative in JS: track the share of days at 4 or 5 in the last 14 against the person's long-run share, with Beta-binomial uncertainty. An ordered-probit is possible in JS but probably overkill for one person. This exceedance approach is my design inference, not a validated method.
usable.note: The flyer text matches: 100% of articles analyzing ordinal data used a metric model, with false alarms, misses and inversions, averaging items does not help, ordered-probit advocated. The survey covered articles mentioning 'Likert' in JPSP, Psychological Science and JEP: General. Abstract level only. Journal, volume and pages could not be confirmed: the flyer gives no citation, the Elsevier link returned only a redirect, Crossref returned 429, and the WebSearch budget for this run was exhausted.

usable.claim: The MAD result depends on where the person's mean sits. At mean 3.25 I got 33.9% and 26.6% at SD .8, and 80.7% and 87.4% at SD .5. State the assumed mean of 3.
usable.values: Modified Z = 0.6745 (x - median) / MAD, flag above 3.5 in absolute value. My simulation of rounded 1 to 5 ratings with AR(1) .3: MAD was 0 in 35% of 14-day and 31% of 28-day windows at within-person SD 0.8, and in 88 to 96% at SD 0.5.
usable.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, section 1.3.5.17, Detection of Outliers (citing Iglewicz and Hoaglin).
usable.population: General statistics guidance, not human self-report.
usable.implication: Use the median for the center, but do not rely on plain MAD for scale on one item. Apply it to a multi-item composite (energy, stress, mood, sleep quality), which has more distinct values, and set a scale floor. The simulation is mine and synthetic. Leys et al. 2013, the usual citation for MAD over SD, was not opened.
usable.note: NIST formula, 0.6745 constant, 3.5 cut-off and the Iglewicz and Hoaglin citation are confirmed. NIST says nothing about MAD = 0, so that part rests only on the researcher's simulation. My in-memory rerun at mean 3 agrees: 34.8% and 30.0% at SD .8, and 87.7% and 95.8% at SD .5 (14 and 28 days).

usable.claim: The 190 to 1,680 figures are illustrative: a CUSUM for a one-sigma upward shift with baseline mean and SD each off by plus or minus one standard error. Changepoint monitoring is the authors' proposal, not an accepted standard. The simulated rates are one-sided; two-sided rates were about double (17.6, 12.0, 9.2 on continuous AR .3 data).
usable.values: With a baseline of n = 100, actual in-control average run length ranged 190 to 1,680 against a nominal 500. My simulation (latent AR(1) .3, CUSUM k .5, h 4): 7.7 false alarms a year from a 14-day baseline, 5.5 from 28, 4.4 from 60. With no autocorrelation: 4.1, 2.5, 1.7.
usable.source: Hawkins DM, Qiu P, Kang CW (2003). The Changepoint Model for Statistical Process Control. J Quality Technology 35(4):355. First three pages read.
usable.population: Industrial process monitoring, not people.
usable.implication: A 14 to 28 day personal baseline cannot give a known false alarm rate. Keep updating the baseline, use predictive limits that widen when data are short, and suppress alerts before about 28 entries. Keep flagged stretches out of the baseline, or a rolling baseline will absorb chronic stress and call it normal (my design inference).
usable.note: Pages 355 to 360 read. Table 1 does show 190 to 1,680 against nominal 500, and the citation is right. 'Accepted way' overstates it: the authors say 'we argue', and page 358 says the formulation 'has not been used extensively' in SPC. 'Self-starting' does not appear in the pages read. The authors also advise against testing from the third reading; they assume 9 untested readings, then testing from the 10th. My rerun matched the simulation only for a one-sided chart: rounded ratings at SD .8 gave 7.8, 5.5, 4.3, and independent continuous data gave 4.1, 2.5, 1.7. The claim's own inputs are not fully specified.

usable.claim: My continuous-data rerun gave median delays of 7 to 14 days for CUSUM and 8 to 12 for EWMA. The doubling holds for CUSUM; EWMA rose about 1.5 times. All alarm rates are one-sided.
usable.values: EWMA: lambda .2 to .3 (NIST calls the choice somewhat arbitrary), limits about plus or minus 3 s sqrt(lambda/(2-lambda)). CUSUM: k is half the shift, h about 4 to 5. My simulation, 28-day baseline, AR .3: EWMA .2/L3 gave 3.0 alarms a year, CUSUM h4 gave 5.5, EWMA .1/L3.5 gave 1.6, CUSUM h8 gave 1.3. Stricter settings doubled median delay for a sustained +1 SD shift from 6 to 12-13 days.
usable.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, EWMA section 6.3.2.4 and CUSUM section https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmc/section3/pmc323.htm. Autocorrelation: Osei-Aning R, Abbasi SA, Riaz M (2017), Scientia Iranica 24(3):1603-1614, https://pure.kfupm.edu.sa/en/publications/monitoring-of-serially-correlated-processes-using-residual-contro/ (abstract only).
usable.population: Industrial data. No validation on human self-report.
usable.implication: Start with EWMA lambda about .1 (half-life about 6.6 days) and L about 3.5, or CUSUM h about 8, on a composite, one-sided toward worsening. This gives about one or two false alarms a year at the cost of about two weeks' lag, which suits slow drift. These settings come from my synthetic simulation, not published validation. An EWMA is the same computation as a leaky integrator.
usable.note: NIST confirmed: lambda usually .2 to .3, 'somewhat arbitrary', k usually 3 in the limit formula, CUSUM k half the shift, h around 4 or 5. The EWMA page states independence, and normality for the Lucas and Saccucci tables; the CUSUM page does not state these assumptions. Osei-Aning abstract confirms false alarms under autocorrelation. Rerun with rounded ratings at SD .8, one-sided: 3.1, 5.5, 1.6, 1.2, close to the claim. The need for stricter settings is the researcher's inference, not in these sources.

usable.claim: Control charts for monitoring one patient have a small, positive evidence base, none of it found for mood, stress or burnout.
usable.values: 7 of 74 identified studies met inclusion. Three studies of about 35 to 45 patients reported good sensitivity and specificity. Four case studies were anecdotal.
usable.source: Tennant R, Mohammed MA, Coleman JJ, Martin U (2007). Monitoring patients using control charts: a systematic review. Int J Qual Health Care 19(4):187-194. Abstract only.
usable.population: Patients with hypertension, asthma, renal transplant or diabetes, on clinical measures rather than self-rated mood.
usable.implication: Personal charting is a reasonable method but an extrapolation for GrowLog. Describe it as a personal trend check, not a validated burnout detector.
usable.note: Abstract page confirms 74 identified and 7 included, three performance studies with n = 35 to 45 reporting good sensitivity and specificity, and four anecdotal case studies. Conditions match. The authors call the role promising but largely under-researched and ask for rigorous evaluation.

usable.claim: CORDIS says SPC accuracy was higher than EWS for transitions toward higher depressive symptoms, gives no numbers, and says only that it 'may hold promise'. Helmich's abstract says 'little support', not 'weak'.
usable.values: Signals preceded transitions in 32.9% with a transition vs 16.2% without. Requiring at least 3 affect measures: 52.6% true positives, 11.1% false positives. Therapy sample: about 44% vs 27%. At-risk youth: about 5% sensitivity, about 96 specificity as printed. Helmich 2024 calls the evidence weak.
usable.source: TRANS-ID project periodic report, EU CORDIS grant 681466 (not peer reviewed; the SPC comparison has no numbers there). Helmich MA, Schreuder MJ, Bringmann LF, Riese H, Snippe E, Smit AC (2024), Nat Rev Psychol 3(11):767-780, abstract at https://research.tilburguniversity.edu/en/publications/slow-down-and-be-critical-before-using-early-warning-signals-in-p/. Smit AC, et al. (2025), Clin Psychol Sci 13(4):760-773, abstract at https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/clinical/21677026241305136/.
usable.population: Formerly depressed adults tapering antidepressants (37 in Smit 2025, about 524 assessments each at 5 a day), depressed patients starting therapy, at-risk youth. Not burnout.
usable.implication: Do not build a rising-autocorrelation alarm. These studies used hundreds of assessments, far beyond one rating a day for a few weeks. Detect sustained mean shifts instead.
usable.note: All CORDIS figures match: 32.9 vs 16.2, 52.6 and 11.1, about 44 vs 27, about 5% and about 96. The report is a periodic report and says EWS were not consistent enough as a clinical monitoring tool. Smit 2025 confirmed: 37 participants, average 524 assessments, 5 a day. Helmich citation confirmed.

usable.claim: Beyond a person's mean and variability of affect, more complex dynamics such as inertia add little for predicting well-being.
usable.values: 15 studies, 1,777 participants. Dynamic measures offered little added value beyond mean and variance.
usable.source: Dejonckheere E, Mestdagh M, Houben M, et al. (2019). Complex affect dynamics add limited information to the prediction of psychological well-being. Nat Hum Behav 3:478-491. Abstract only.
usable.population: Pooled affective time series from 15 studies, n = 1,777. Between-person prediction of life satisfaction, depressive and borderline symptoms, not within-person burnout onset.
usable.implication: Keep the model to level and spread. Skip inertia, instability and network metrics, which also cannot be estimated reliably from sparse single-person data.
usable.note: Abstract confirms 15 studies, n = 1,777, outcomes of life satisfaction, depressive and borderline symptoms, and little added value of dynamics beyond mean and variance. Citation is 3(5):478-491.

usable.claim: One of six in a small depression study is weak evidence on how common sudden transitions are. 'A step-change detector should not be the core method' is the researcher's inference, not a finding of either source.
usable.values: A significant sudden transition was found in 1 of 6 participants. Signals rose about one month earlier in that one case, which is not a sensitivity estimate.
usable.source: Wichers M, Smit AC, Snippe E (2020). J Pers Oriented Res 6(1):1-15, abstract only. Adams RP, MacKay DJC (2007). Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection, arXiv 0710.3742, abstract only, https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3742.
usable.population: Six single-subject time series, 3 ratings a day for 95 to 183 days, in depression research.
usable.implication: Prefer EWMA for gradual drift. Bayesian online changepoint detection is exact and online, and tracking run length with a capped window should be feasible in plain JS, but I found no validation on daily mood or burnout self-report. Treat it as an optional later extra.
usable.note: Abstract read through NCBI's record service because the PubMed page returned a cookie notice. Confirmed: six single-subject studies, 3 ratings a day for 95 to 183 days, one significant sudden transition, signals rising a month before. The abstract does not discuss what happened in the other five. The source does not address detector choice; its message is that signals can expose a nearby transition. Adams and MacKay is a methods abstract and says nothing about how common transitions are.

usable.claim: The prediction failure comes from Busso, whose abstract does not call the 11 swimmers elite, so 'even in elite athletes' is not established for it. The statistic is mean absolute percentage error: 2.02% plus or minus .65 and 2.69% plus or minus 1.23.
usable.values: Time parameters with 95% bootstrap CI: t(a) 38 (17-59), t(f) 19 (6-32), t(n) 19 (7-35), t(g) 43 (25-61). R2 .79 plus or minus .13 in fit. Busso 2023: mean absolute error 2.02% and 2.69% on validation sets, judged not satisfactory for individual planning.
usable.source: Hellard P, et al. (2006). Assessing the limitations of the Banister model in monitoring training. J Sports Sci 24(5):509-520. Also Busso T, Chalencon S (2023), Med Sci Sports Exerc 55, abstract at https://lida.sport-iat.de/ta/Record/4082486?lng=en. Abstracts only.
usable.population: 9 elite swimmers over one season; 11 swimmers over 61 weeks. No cognitive load and no self-rated stress.
usable.implication: Do not fit personal Banister parameters. GrowLog has no measured performance outcome and far fewer events, so identifiability would be worse. Fixed decay constants are the feasible option, stated openly as assumptions.
usable.note: Hellard confirmed through the NCBI record: nine elite swimmers, the four time parameters with 95% bootstrap CIs, R2 .79 plus or minus .13, wide intervals, highly correlated parameters. It also says estimation seemed stable, and it does not test forecasting. Busso confirmed: 11 swimmers, 61 weeks, values for the Banister model, and prediction not satisfactory for individual training planning.

usable.claim: The authors call the association small-to-moderate. Injury type was a significant moderator (p = .01), and time-loss injuries were near null (g = .01).
usable.values: g = .35 (95% CI .16 to .54), I2 = 95.8%. Rolling vs EWMA method, time window and load metric were non-significant moderators. Authors warn against universal thresholds.
usable.source: Ding L, et al. (2026). Acute:chronic workload ratio and load management for team sports: a multilevel meta-analysis. Front Public Health. Also Impellizzeri FM, et al. (2020), IJSPP 15(6):907-913, abstract at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32502973.
usable.population: Team-sport athletes: 41 studies reviewed, 16 pooled, 797 athletes. Injury outcomes, not burnout.
usable.implication: Do not port a ratio or a 0.8 to 1.3 sweet-spot band to study or development minutes. If load is shown, show it against the person's own usual as context. 7-day and 28-day windows are convention, not evidence.
usable.note: Full text read. g = .35 (95% CI .16 to .54), I2 = 95.8%, 41 reviewed, 16 pooled, 797 athletes. Method, window and load metric were non-significant moderators, and the authors reject stand-alone use and universal thresholds. Impellizzeri abstract confirms artifacts and citation.

usable.claim: Veldhuis is not a qualitative model. It is a quantitative stock-and-flow model with equations and accumulating stocks, including capacity for effort and stress. Its validation is qualitative, with no fitted parameters reported. Eight employees were recruited, but only seven completed the sketches.
usable.values: Veldhuis gives no numeric time constants; simulated 100 weeks; case timelines about 1 to 3 years, some 10. De Bloom: d = +.43 during vacation, d = -.38 fade-out after work resumes, no time scale in the abstract.
usable.source: Veldhuis GA, et al. (2020). A Proof-of-Concept System Dynamics Simulation Model of the Development of Burnout and Recovery Using Retrospective Case Data. Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(16):5964. Also de Bloom J, et al. (2009), J Occup Health 51(1):13-25, abstract at https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/joh/51/1/51_K8004/_article.
usable.population: 8 employees of one Dutch institute giving retrospective sketches, plus 5 experts. De Bloom: workers in 7 vacation studies.
usable.implication: Any stress total in GrowLog is descriptive, not a validated burnout quantity. Treat decay as a stated design assumption, for example EWMAs near 7 and 28 days. Timelines of months to years suggest a few bad weeks should not be labeled burnout.
usable.note: Confirmed for Veldhuis: no numeric time constants in the text read, 100-week simulation, timelines of about 1 to 3 years with some up to 10, five experts, and a statement that longitudinal studies are needed. De Bloom confirmed: d = +.43 and -.38, 7 studies, no time scale in the abstract. The opening statement that no fitted accumulation model exists could not be checked, because the WebSearch budget for this run was exhausted.

usable.claim: Personal-baseline anomaly detection before relapse has been shown only on a handful of events, and data near the event often go missing because people stop using the app.
usable.values: 5 of 15 relapsed, and only 3 had enough pre-relapse data. The other 2 stopped using the app 1 to 3 weeks before hospitalization. Anomalies 10/118 (.085/day) before relapse vs 8/161 (.050/day) otherwise, reported as 71% higher.
usable.source: Barnett I, Torous J, Staples P, et al. (2018). Relapse prediction in schizophrenia through digital phenotyping: a pilot study. Neuropsychopharmacology.
usable.population: 15 outpatients with schizophrenia analyzed, 1,075 person-days, median 79 days. Not burnout.
usable.implication: Expect event-adjacent gaps. Let users mark a burnout event after the fact, with a fuzzy date, and treat a logging stop as a noteworthy marker. The method's rank transform and weekly detrending are cheap in JS, but this result does not show prediction.
usable.note: The first two tries returned a verification page; the plain article URL then loaded and I read the text. 17 enrolled, 15 analyzed, 1,075 person-days, median 79 days, 5 relapsed, 3 with enough data. One person uninstalled 3 weeks before hospitalization, the other 1 week before. 10 of 118 vs 8 of 161, .085 vs .050 a day, 71% higher. The paper describes the counts as tests. The word 'only' reaches beyond this one pilot.

usable.claim: Add that healthy controls appear to be in the evaluation: the Discussion says over a quarter of those with paired anomalies were controls and links this to the PPV. The relapse criteria tallies were 4, 2 and 23, with overlap unstated.
usable.values: Sensitivity 89%, specificity 75%, PPV 60%, NPV 94%. No held-out test set described. Relapse total not stated; about 27 implied, and the paper's counts do not fully reconcile.
usable.source: Henson P, D'Mello R, Vaidyam A, Keshavan M, Torous J (2021). Anomaly detection to predict relapse risk in schizophrenia. Transl Psychiatry.
usable.population: 90 analyzed: 63 with schizophrenia, 27 healthy controls, Boston. Relapse was mostly clinician-judged care increases, and some dates were imprecise.
usable.implication: My calculation: with one event a year and a 14-day pre-event window (prevalence 3.8%), those figures give PPV of about 12%, and even 80% sensitivity with 90% specificity gives about 24%. So most flags would be false. Say 'higher than your usual', never 'burnout is coming'.
usable.note: Full text read. 90 of 126 analyzed, 63 with schizophrenia and 27 controls, 89%, 75%, 60%, 94%. No hold-out or cross-validation described, and no relapse total stated. Back-calculated counts sum to 91, as the claim says. The collapse at low base rates is the researcher's inference. My arithmetic gives PPV of about 16% at a 5% base rate.

usable.claim: The three figures count patients, not events, so the implied events are about 180, 375 and 298 by my calculation. They hold only for those settings: 10 predictors in the simulation, 23 predictor parameters in MIMIC-III, and 15% of maximum Cox-Snell R2.
usable.values: Minimum sample 898 at 20% prevalence, 749 at 50%, 2,590 at 11.5% mortality, targeting shrinkage above .9. My t-based calculation: a 95% prediction interval for the next event's level from n past events is about plus or minus 15.6 SD at n=2, 5.0 at n=3, 3.0 at n=5, 2.4 at n=10.
usable.source: Martin GP, Riley RD, Collins GS, Sperrin M (2021). Developing clinical prediction models when adhering to minimum sample size recommendations. Stat Methods Med Res 30(12):2545-2561.
usable.population: Simulation and a critical-care example. Population models, not single-person models.
usable.implication: Do not train a personal classifier on burnout labels, and do not set a threshold from one or two events. Use events only to move a prior slowly. Suggested gates, which are my convention: show a personal marker at 3 or more events as a range, and let it influence alerts only at 5 or more. No published minimum for one person was found.
usable.note: Full text read. 898, 749 and 2,590 are confirmed, as are shrinkage above .9, penalization not justifying inadequate samples, and the 10-events rule being overly simplistic. Prediction-interval values recomputed: 15.56, 4.97, 3.04, 2.37. The single-person application is the researcher's inference.

usable.claim: The 2-week test ran over 58 leave-one-out iterations, and each person's first 2 weeks were pooled with all other patients' data. It therefore needs population data, which a phone-only single user lacks. The paper's Discussion gives .547 where Results and Table 3 give .347.
usable.values: Leave-all-out R2: hierarchical .511, repeat-last-day .342, personal mean .213. With only 2 weeks of a new person's data, separate personal models gave negative R2 and the hierarchical model roughly equalled pooled models. No learning curve was reported.
usable.source: Busk J, et al. (2020). Forecasting Mood in Bipolar Disorder From Smartphone Self-assessments: Hierarchical Bayesian Approach. JMIR mHealth uHealth. Closed-form updates: Murphy KP (2007), Conjugate Bayesian analysis of the Gaussian distribution, https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~murphyk/Papers/bayesGauss.pdf (pages 1 to 3 read).
usable.population: 84 people with bipolar disorder in the MONARCA II trial, 15,975 daily self-ratings, one month ahead not tested. Multi-user cohort, not a single-user setting.
usable.implication: Full hierarchical fitting is not needed on the phone. Hard-code a population prior and update it in closed form: weight on own mean = n/(n + k), where k = (1-ICC)/ICC, about 1.2 to 2.6 pseudo-days from I2, so the prior on the mean fades within a week. Keep a stronger prior on the variance. Recommended stack, all constant-time per day in plain JS with localStorage: Beta-binomial counts for high days, a composite EWMA with t-based limits, and event markers stored as ranges. Always test against 'same as yesterday'.
usable.note: Full text read. 84 patients, 15,975 self-assessments, leave-all-out R2 .511, .342, .213 ('separate mean' is the paper's label for personal mean). With 2 weeks: hierarchical .347, pooled .343 and .340, separate models negative. Horizons up to 7 days. No learning curve. Murphy 2007 pages 1 to 3 confirm closed-form updates.

usable.claim: Missing days may be informative, but the evidence conflicts. One study found higher stress and negative affect predicted missing the next prompt, while a major review reports little evidence that momentary states affect compliance.
usable.values: Higher stress, negative affect and feeling upset predicted missing the next prompt; odds ratios not seen. Typical compliance 70 to 85%. About 75% within-person compliance is custom, and the review says that is hard to justify. Most evidence comes from the prompt before, not the missed moment itself.
usable.source: Murray AL, et al. (2023). Prompt-level predictors of compliance in an ecological momentary assessment study of young adults' mental health. J Affect Disord (abstract only). Stone AA, Schneider S, Smyth JM. Evaluation of Pressing Issues in Ecological Momentary Assessment. Annu Rev Clin Psychol 19:107-131, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12991416/.
usable.population: 260 general-population young adults in the D2M study (country not stated). The review covers mixed behavioral and medical EMA studies.
usable.implication: Never impute a gap as neutral or as the person's average, and do not let stress totals quietly decay across gaps. Show the state as unknown after about 3 missed days, offer a one-tap catch-up, and restart the short window after long gaps. These cutoffs are my design choices.
usable.note: Murray abstract confirmed: 260 young adults in D2M; stress, negative affect and feeling upset predicted missing the next prompt; no odds ratios shown; country not stated. Citation is 322:125-131. Stone review read: 70 to 85%, the 75% custom described as an impression, 'little evidence' on momentary experiences, and evidence mostly from the previous prompt. Published online 2022, volume 19 dated 2023. Both sources concern momentary prompts, so applying them to missed daily entries is an extrapolation.

usable.claim: Most users of mental health apps leave before any personal baseline could form, although tracker apps retain somewhat better.
usable.values: Median retention 3.9% at day 15 and 3.3% at day 30. Tracker apps 6.1% at day 30.
usable.source: Baumel A, Muench F, Edan S, Kane JM (2019). Objective User Engagement With Mental Health Apps: Systematic Search and Panel-Based Usage Analysis. J Med Internet Res 21(9):e14567. Abstract only.
usable.population: 93 Android apps with 10,000 or more installs, aggregated panel usage data. A different product mix from GrowLog.
usable.implication: Defaults must work alone from day 1, and most users will never reach personal thresholds or log an event. Make personalization visible early with milestones at about 7, 14 and 28 entries.
usable.note: Abstract page confirms 93 apps with 10,000 or more installs, medians 3.9% at day 15 and 3.3% at day 30, trackers 6.1% at day 30, from aggregated panel data. IQRs are wide (tracker IQR 20.4%). The link to forming a baseline is the researcher's inference.

usable.claim: The 14-day weighted comparison applies to Oura's balance contributors, not to every Readiness contributor. The Readiness Score page says two months generally, while the Contributors page says three months for HRV.
usable.values: Oura: past 2 to 5 days weigh more; bands 85-100, 70-84, 60-69, 0-59. WHOOP: day 4 and day 30, unverified at source.
usable.source: Oura help pages: Readiness Contributors and Readiness Score, https://support.ouraring.com/hc/en-us/articles/360025589793-Readiness-Score. WHOOP: support-page wording was seen only in search results (pages returned 401 or a load error); https://developer.whoop.com/docs/whoop-101/ gives no window; https://www.community.whoop.com/t/how-long-does-it-take-for-whoop-to-learn-your-baseline-metrics/359 is a user post.
usable.population: Wearable customers, physiological signals. No published evidence for these windows was found.
usable.implication: A staged scheme of a first read within 4 to 14 days and a long baseline of 30 to 60 days matches industry practice, but it is convention, not evidence. Copying the two-window structure is defensible; citing it as validated is not.
usable.note: Oura pages confirm a learning period of up to two weeks, two-month long-term average, three months for HRV Balance, last 2 to 5 days counting slightly more, and the four bands. The WHOOP day 4 and 30-day figures appear only in a forum user's post; the developer page gives no window. The Oura details are split across two pages.

usable.claim: Consumer composite scores appear to lack external validation. Body Battery is a charge-and-drain model built on Firstbeat analytics with no independent validation found, and Apple's State of Mind is plain self-report with no personal baseline described.
usable.values: Per the blog: 14 scores from 10 manufacturers; HRV in 86%, resting HR 79%, activity 71%, sleep 71%; none validated against clinical outcomes; weights undisclosed. Apple valence runs -1 to +1 and separates daily mood from momentary emotion.
usable.source: Secondary summary of Doherty C, et al. (2025), Transl Exerc Biomed 2(2):128-144; the original returned HTTP 405 and was not read. Garmin blog https://www.garmin.com/en-US/blog/fitness/why-your-body-battery-may-struggle-to-charge-when-you-start-to-get-sick/. Firstbeat 2014 white paper https://www.firstbeat.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/Stress-and-recovery_white-paper_20145.pdf (vendor, pages 1 to 8 read). Apple WWDC24 https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10109/.
usable.population: Consumer wearable users. Vendor material plus a blog summary of a review.
usable.implication: There is no validated system to copy. GrowLog can do better on transparency by showing the formula and the data behind each flag. Body Battery's language shows that a battery metaphor is understandable, but it says nothing about validity. Apple's daily mood versus momentary emotion split is a useful labeling distinction.
usable.note: The blog gives 14 scores, 10 manufacturers, 86, 79, 71, 71, no clinical validation, weights undisclosed. Doherty's original returned 405 again, so those figures remain second-hand; Crossref confirms its citation details. Garmin confirms Firstbeat analytics and the drain-and-recharge description. The Firstbeat 2014 vendor paper does not mention Body Battery in the pages I read (1, 2, 8 to 10). Apple confirms -1 to +1, dailyMood vs momentaryEmotion and no baseline. 'No independent validation found' could not be rechecked because the WebSearch budget for this run was exhausted.

usable.claim: The wording is 'little better than randomly selecting', so slightly better than chance, and invalid variables may do worse.
usable.values: The paper illustrates thresholds but gives no method for setting them.
usable.source: Nahum-Shani I, Smith SN, Spring BJ, et al. Just-in-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) in Mobile Health: Key Components and Design Principles. Ann Behav Med, DOI 10.1007/s12160-016-9830-8.
usable.population: Conceptual framework across mobile health behavior change. Not burnout.
usable.implication: Default to no alert. One daily check-in means at most one decision a day, and a weekly review fits slow drift better than push notifications. Offer a small recovery suggestion only when a sustained flag fires, and keep burden low so logging itself does not cause dropout.
usable.note: Full text read. Confirmed: explicit 'provide nothing' option, decision points matched to change in the tailoring variable, missingness possibly signalling fatigue and usable as a tailoring variable, thresholds shown only as symbols with no setting method. The source is Ann Behav Med 52(6):446-462, with the longer title ending 'for Ongoing Health Behavior Support'.

usable.claim: Showing uncertainty as numbers costs little trust. Trust fell only slightly and mostly for verbal hedging, not numeric ranges.
usable.values: N = 5,780. Small decrease in trust, mostly with verbal uncertainty.
usable.source: van der Bles AM, van der Linden S, Freeman ALJ, Spiegelhalter DJ (2020). The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers. PNAS. Abstract only.
usable.population: 5,780 participants across five experiments, including a national sample and a BBC News field experiment. News facts, not personal health feedback.
usable.implication: Show a numeric range and the evidence count, such as a usual range plus the number of entries and events behind it, instead of one precise threshold or vague wording. Applying this to personal feedback is an extrapolation.
usable.note: Abstract page and PNAS full text read: 117(14):7672-7683, N = 5,780, five experiments including a national sample and BBC field experiment. Numeric uncertainty was shown as a range around a point estimate. In experiment 1 it did not significantly reduce trust in numbers (4.31 vs 4.52). The overall meta-analytic effect on trust in numbers was d = -.15, mostly attributed to verbal uncertainty. The authors recommend numeric ranges with a point estimate. Setting is news facts, not personal health feedback.

usable.claim: The prior edition is 지침서-0091-02, dated 2020.11 in the source. '-002' and the day '30' appear in nothing I opened. The self-esteem item is appearance-related self-esteem, not self-esteem in general.
usable.source: MFDS, 의료기기와 개인용 건강관리제품(웰니스) 판단기준 (공무원 지침서, 지침서-0091-03), sections II.5 and III. Landing page: https://mfds.go.kr/brd/m_1059/view.do?seq=15229. Press note: https://www.korea.kr/common/download.do?fileId=198359156&tblKey=GMN
usable.population: Products and software in Korea. Not a population study.
usable.implication: GrowLog stays on the wellness side only if app copy, store text, website and social posts all state an everyday stress, sleep and energy purpose. A disclaimer is unlikely to offset medical claims made elsewhere (my inference from the combined test). This is an officials' guideline, not a statute. Article 60 of the device review regulation allows a formal review request if the team wants certainty.
usable.note: I opened the landing page, the PDF (text extracted locally) and the press note. Section III.1 confirms purpose first and risk as subordinate. III.2 confirms purpose is read objectively from labels, ads, spoken or written statements, structure and sales promotion together. The everyday-use list is in III.3 and the no-disease condition is in II.5. The press note confirms the revision on 2026-02-12. Two details fail. The guideline's revision table lists the prior edition as 지침서-0091-02 dated only 2020.11, and the landing page names no replaced document. Context the claim omits: the front matter says this is an internal officials' guideline with no external legal force, valid as of February 2026, and its examples may apply differently by product. Web search budget ran out, so I could not look up the earlier edition's own page.

usable.claim: MFDS case tables place this on the wellness side: non-medical software for stress relief that offers a self-report questionnaire widely used in academia, records emotional state, and gives personalised content on music, meditation, essays, diet and sleep. The device side has tailored cognitive therapy for insomnia patients, tailored treatment content for panic disorder patients, and emotion logs stored, sent or analysed for clinical care at medical institutions.
usable.source: MFDS, 지침서-0091-03, section IV.3, pages 19 to 21
usable.population: Actual MFDS classification cases. Not a population study.
usable.implication: Self-rating plus personalised everyday suggestions is the closest precedent, so learning personal baselines should not by itself cross the line (my inference, not an MFDS ruling on GrowLog). The line is drawn by targeting patients, tailoring treatment, or feeding clinical care. Do not build a 'report for your doctor' feature without review. A user's own plain export is a separate question I could not resolve.
usable.note: All entries are in IV.3 at printed pages 19 to 21, and the press note confirms they come from real inquiry cases. The wellness entry requires a non-medical purpose and a stress-relief aim, and describes a paper-and-pencil self-diagnosis questionnaire, so 'self-report' is a gloss. The insomnia entry also mentions real-time behavioural intervention messages. The panic entry concerns symptom improvement with difficulty-adjusted content, and a separate panic entry for non-medical breathing training sits on the wellness side. The device-side emotion log is an AI voice-chat app for patients, including older adults. A non-medical AI app recording older adults' emotions sits on the wellness side.

usable.claim: MFDS treats a product as high risk, and so not wellness, if it detects emergencies such as cardiac arrest or death, or if failure to work as intended could cause injury or illness. A sleep device measuring apnoea is listed as high risk, and an app with alarms for dangerous glucose values appears on the device side.
usable.source: MFDS, 지침서-0091-03, section III.2 and III.3 (risk questions) and section IV.3, pages 12 to 15 and 19
usable.population: Products in Korea. Not a population study.
usable.implication: Do not build or describe GrowLog as detecting a suicide crisis, or as a danger alarm for burnout. Reliance on such a feature creates the failure risk these questions target (my inference by analogy; MFDS has no case on self-rated mood). Show crisis contacts as general information that is always available, and state that the app does not watch for emergencies.
usable.note: Confirmed in III.2 and III.3 at printed pages 12 to 15, and the table of contents numbers run one lower than the page footers. The apnoea device is listed under injury or illness from unintended operation. The glucose entry on page 19 is for diabetes patients and combines periodic numeric readings and recording with data transmission or a danger-value alarm, so it is not an alarm alone. The low-risk examples on page 13 include a diet tracker that warns users about overeating, so a warning by itself does not make a product high risk.

usable.claim: The sentence naming screening or diagnosis of a disease or condition sits in the II.5 sub-bullet on blood pressure and glucose. The general exclusion in II.5 refers to medical use such as diagnosis or checking treatment timing.
usable.values: KCD listing is unofficial and states no KCD edition.
usable.source: MFDS, 지침서-0091-03, section II.1, II.3 and II.5. KCD listing (third party, weak source): https://kcd.epostphone.kr/code/Z730
usable.population: Products in Korea. Not a population study.
usable.implication: MFDS has not ruled on a burnout index, so this list is my inference. Avoid 번아웃 진단, 번아웃 예측, 번아웃 예방, 우울증 위험, 치료, 증상 개선, 정상/비정상, 위험 수치. Prefer 오늘의 부하와 회복, 내 평소와 비교, 쉬어가기 제안. A KCD code could put 'burnout' inside MFDS's disease test despite WHO's wording, so the index should not be named as a burnout measure. The word 'risk' alone is not decisive: a fall-risk product is listed as wellness, and the disease reference is what matters.
usable.note: The diagnosis, prevention and disease definitions match the table in II.1, including the KCD test for disease. The CaseNote-independent KCD lookup page lists Z73.0 as problems related to burn-out, also as vital exhaustion, under Z73, and names no edition. It gives a disease-master reference date of 2025-09-30. The researcher's weak-source label is right. No source I read says burnout is a disease for MFDS purposes, so that should not be inferred from Z73.0 appearing in the KCD.

usable.claim: WHO defines burn-out as a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with three dimensions: exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced professional efficacy. WHO says it is 'not classified as a medical condition' and applies only to the occupational context.
usable.values: ICD-11 QD85 per search metadata, not stated in the text I read.
usable.source: WHO, Burn-out an occupational phenomenon, ICD-11 FAQ
usable.population: Global classification. Occupational context only.
usable.implication: An exhaustion-only index does not measure WHO's construct, and students fall outside WHO's scope. Honest copy should say GrowLog shows load and recovery patterns, not burnout. The user-logged event should be phrased as the person's own experience, such as 내가 많이 지쳤던 날, not as a confirmed burnout episode.
usable.note: The WHO page matches on the definition, the three dimensions and the phrase 'not classified as a medical condition'. It says the concept should not describe other areas of life. It does not mention QD85, as the researcher said.

usable.claim: Korea's Medical Devices Act Article 26 paragraph 7 bars anyone from labelling or advertising a non-device product in a way that could lead people to think it has device-like performance, efficacy or effects. Selling or leasing such a product, or storing or displaying it for that purpose, is also barred.
usable.values: Text read is the version effective 2027-10-21 (Act 22105). I did not confirm the current in-force wording or the penalty.
usable.source: 의료기기법 제26조제7항, national law information centre. Second copy: https://www.law.go.kr/LSW//lsLawLinkInfo.do?lsJoLnkSeq=1000067611&lsId=009514&chrClsCd=010202&print=print
usable.population: Anyone labelling or advertising a non-device product in Korea.
usable.implication: Treat this as the main legal exposure from copy. Being free does not obviously remove the advertising ban, since it applies to anyone (my reading, not legal advice). Review the store page, landing page and share images, not only in-app text. Do not write 임상적으로 검증, or imply that the score works like a clinical test.
usable.note: Both law.go.kr links show Act 22105, promulgated 2026-10-20 and effective 2027-10-21, with the wording claimed. The researcher's gap can be narrowed. The MFDS guideline of February 2026 reprints the same paragraph, and CaseNote's Article 26 (Act 21949, effective 2027-03-16) shows it unchanged, with only a new paragraph 8 added. On penalty, CaseNote's Article 52(1)1 cites Article 26 paragraphs 2 to 7: up to 3 years or 30 million won, and the two can be combined. That text is a third-party copy marked effective 2025-02-09, and law.go.kr's own article pages would not load, so confirm before relying on it. Guideline section V.2 adds complaints or administrative guidance as enforcement. The labelling limb names exterior, packaging and package inserts and does not mention apps or software.

usable.claim: Step counts are based on gyroscope or accelerometer sensors. State the designation list as of January 2026.
usable.values: MFDS plans to extend designation to exercise, diet and mental health promotion products. False or exaggerated advertising that seriously harms or threatens public health can bring recall, sales suspension and publication.
usable.source: MFDS announcement relayed by BioIN, 식약처 디지털의료·건강지원기기 제도 시행 (2026-01-26). Definition: MFDS 지침서-0091-03 section II.4.
usable.population: Non-device digital health products in Korea.
usable.implication: A self-report app that uses no sensors does not appear to be designated, so no filing seems needed today. Its description already fits the statutory wording, so recheck the designation notice at least yearly. I did not open the designation notice itself.
usable.note: The BioIN post dated 2026-01-26 reposts the MFDS release and confirms the phase dates, the four indicators, voluntary reporting and certification, the planned extension and the sanctions. It names mobile apps as an example form. MFDS section II.4 confirms the designation limit. BioIN does not say how undesignated products are treated. 'So far' is only true as of January 2026. This session's web search budget ran out, so I could not check for later designations; a follow-up search would allow that check.

usable.claim: The FDA's January 2026 General Wellness guidance, which MFDS says it partly reflected, states a product can stay in wellness while telling users that professional evaluation may be helpful when outputs fall outside wellness ranges. The notification must not name a disease, must not call the output abnormal, pathological or diagnostic, must not include clinical thresholds, diagnoses or treatment advice, and must not provide ongoing alerts to manage a condition.
usable.values: The same passage allows values, ranges, trends, baselines and longitudinal summaries in relation to sleep, activity, stress and recovery, within the non-invasive sensing discussion. MFDS's note names only the glucose and blood pressure graph change as adopted.
usable.source: FDA, General Wellness: Policy for Low Risk Devices, issued 2026-01-06, section III. MFDS press note on partial reflection: https://www.korea.kr/common/download.do?fileId=198359156&tblKey=GMN
usable.population: US products. Nonbinding guidance, not Korean law.
usable.implication: Best available template for a 'talk to someone' prompt: for example 요즘 힘든 날이 이어졌네요. 누군가와 이야기해 보는 것도 도움이 될 수 있어요. No disease name, no score cut-off shown, no word 비정상. Personal baselines are in line with this text. Do not copy FDA's example of 'living well with anxiety', because MFDS's list of chronic conditions (heart disease, hypertension, hypotension, type 2 diabetes) does not include anxiety.
usable.note: Text extracted from the FDA PDF: issued January 6, 2026, section III. The four notification conditions match, and the fourth reads ongoing alerts or monitoring. The values and baselines sentence applies to products meeting the non-invasive sensing criteria. The press note footnote names only the blood pressure and glucose graph change as reflected. Important limit: the MFDS guideline contains no equivalent of this notification allowance, so it is not a Korean safe harbour. The guideline does bar guiding specific clinical action in its blood pressure and glucose passage. Section V.3 recommends a caution that the product cannot judge disease and that a doctor's examination is needed. Nearby FDA text also excludes products whose labelling or interface refers to diagnostic thresholds.

usable.claim: Neither source compares MHRA with MFDS, so 'stricter' is the researcher's inference. MHRA's test covers conditions and/or symptoms at levels considered diagnosable or clinically relevant, which is wider than 'conditions at diagnosable levels'.
usable.values: Example 6: a wellbeing claim on the website plus social media implying reduced depression risk gives an inferred medical purpose.
usable.source: MHRA, Digital Mental Health Technology: device characterisation, regulatory qualification and classification, version 1.3 (revision dated 2026-07-29), section 6.1 and Tables 1 and 2
usable.population: UK products. Not Korean law.
usable.implication: Use this as a conservative outer limit. It matters most if GrowLog ever markets abroad. Label the stress rating as a daily stress rating, not anxiety tracking. Prefer not to embed PHQ-9 or GAD-7. Although MFDS accepts academic self-tests for stress relief, this is the cleaner option under both regimes.
usable.note: Text extracted from the PDF. Version 1.3 and the 2026-07-29 revision are confirmed, though that revision changed only the wording of function 11. Table 1 lists tracking and graphs under monitoring. The anxiety and sports contrast matches section 6.1.2, with the sports case requiring no inferred medical benefit. The PHQ-9 and GAD-7 point is in Table 2 Note 1, and relapse or crisis prediction is in Table 2. Example 6 matches, and it also offers regular recommendation by healthcare professionals as an alternative trigger.

usable.claim: The personal-contacts statement is on page 18, not pages 19 to 21.
usable.values: Statute as read took effect 2023-09-15. Casenote also lists Act 21910, effective 2027-03-09, which I did not read.
usable.source: PIPC, 개인정보 보호법령 해석 실무 교재 (2021.11, third-party copy), pp. 19 to 21 and 163. Statute: https://casenote.kr/%EB%B2%95%EB%A0%B9/%EA%B0%9C%EC%9D%B8%EC%A0%95%EB%B3%B4_%EB%B3%B4%ED%98%B8%EB%B2%95/%EC%A0%9C2%EC%A1%B0 . Sensitive data: https://www.easylaw.go.kr/CSP/CnpClsMainBtr.laf?popMenu=ov&csmSeq=1257&ccfNo=2&cciNo=3&cnpClsNo=1 . 대법원 2023도5226: https://casenote.kr/%EB%8C%80%EB%B2%95%EC%9B%90/2023%EB%8F%845226
usable.population: Personal data processing in Korea.
usable.implication: 'Free' is not a shield. The strongest position is that the developer holds no file and never receives data, while the user's own logging is personal use. That is my inference: I found no PIPC ruling on an on-device-only app. Daily mood and stress ratings are not expressly covered, so handle them as sensitive. Any cloud backup, sync, server analytics or crash reporting that receives this data could change the analysis, and would need separate consent and safety measures, so get advice first.
usable.note: The third-party PDF has no extractable text, so I read rendered pages. The cover confirms PIPC, November 2021. Page 19 says work does not depend on pay or profit, and that duties are limited to those operating a file. It adds that even a single act can count if there is intent to continue. Page 163 gives the health-information description, with disability grade status and blood type excluded. CaseNote confirms Article 2(5), effective 2023-09-15, and lists Act 21910. Easylaw confirms separate consent and safety measures, but it only lists health as a category. The material predates the 2023 amendment. CaseNote shows Article 23 in a newer version (Act 21445, effective 2026-09-11). The Supreme Court case cited concerns Article 59 and 'in the course of business', and does not directly address on-device apps.

usable.claim: The PIPC's April 2026 privacy policy guideline, as summarised by Korean law firms, says that where data is processed only on the user's device, it is recommended to disclose that personal data is not sent to external servers. If data is stored on a server, the purpose, items, retention period and legal basis must be listed. Incidental device logs, usage patterns or crash reports sent to a server are likely to make it a hybrid type.
usable.values: Published 2026-04-24. The official PDF was too large to open, so these are law-firm summaries.
usable.source: 대륙아주 newsletter in Law Times on 2026 개인정보 처리방침 작성지침. 화우 newsletter: https://www.lawtimes.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=220000 . Official listing: https://www.privacy.go.kr/front/bbs/bbsView.do?bbsNo=BBSMSTR_000000000049&bbscttNo=20885
usable.population: Controllers and on-device services in Korea.
usable.implication: Publish a short plain statement: records stay in this browser on this phone and are not sent to the developer. Before saying so, audit the PWA for host logs, analytics, fonts and third-party scripts. Also tell users that clearing browser data deletes records, and that anyone with the phone can read them.
usable.note: Supported only as law-firm reporting. The Law Times piece under 대륙아주 (published 2026-05-14) supports the server-stored list and the recommended on-device disclosure. The 화우 piece (2026-04-27) alone supports the hybrid sentence. The privacy.go.kr listing confirms the title and the date 2026-04-24. The official PDF exceeded the fetch size limit for me too, so the guideline's own wording remains unverified. Both pieces are Law Times law-firm articles, and 'newsletter' is a loose label. The word 'hybrid' here is the firm's reading, so check it against the official PDF before any legal decision.

usable.claim: 129.go.kr does give hours for 1577-0199, describing it as 24-hour mental health counselling. Only the MOHW page omits hours.
usable.values: Verified 2026-10-31. MOHW page last updated 2025-08-19 and gives no hours for 1577-0199. Its 129 line is weekdays 09:00 to 18:00 with emergency counselling 24 hours. 109 can dispatch help through 112. A 2023 korea.kr article listed 1577-0199 for consolidation; the current official page supersedes it.
usable.source: Health and Welfare Call Center: https://www.129.go.kr/109 . MOHW: https://www.mohw.go.kr/menu.es?mid=a10706040100 . MOHW press 2024-01-02: https://www.mohw.go.kr/board.es?mid=a10503010100&bid=0027&act=view&list_no=1479607&tag=&nPage=1 . 한국생명존중희망재단: https://www.kfsp.or.kr/ . korea.kr reporter piece 2025-12-15: https://www.korea.kr/news/reporterView.do?newsId=148956325
usable.population: Anyone in Korea.
usable.implication: Show 109 first, as a tap-to-call link, from every screen, labelled 24시간. Show 1577-0199 as 정신건강 상담 without claiming 24 hours unless the team confirms it. Offer 마들랜 for people who cannot phone, and add 112 or 119 for immediate danger. Do not show the retired 1393. Show this to everyone, not only after a low score.
usable.note: 129.go.kr confirms 109, the 2024-01-01 consolidation, and that the other lines keep their own roles, with 1366 named only in the FAQ. The MOHW page confirms 1577-0199 routing, its update date of 2025-08-19, and that it gives no hours. The MOHW press release confirms 112 dispatch, which 129.go.kr does not mention. kfsp.or.kr lists 마들랜 as live online counselling with suicide-prevention counsellors. The 24-hour, free, nickname, app and KakaoTalk details come only from a citizen reporter piece of 2025-12-15, which also says sessions run up to 50 minutes. I could not check the 2023 korea.kr article because no URL was given and the search budget ran out.

usable.claim: A review of 69 depression and suicide prevention apps found 6 gave helpline numbers that were non-existent, non-functional, or linked to an organisation offering non-evidence-based treatment. Two of these apps each had more than a million downloads. Only 5 apps included all six guideline strategies.
usable.values: 6/69 (9%) faulty numbers. 5/69 (7%) all six strategies. Strategies: mood or thought tracking 41%, safety plan 38%, deterring activities 48%, information 51%, support networks 41%, emergency counselling 67%.
usable.source: Martinengo et al., Suicide prevention and depression apps' suicide risk assessment and management, BMC Medicine 2019
usable.population: 69 depression and suicide prevention apps in app stores. Not user outcomes.
usable.implication: Add a release checklist that re-verifies every number on the official page before each release, and show a 'last checked' date. Hosting the numbers in one file makes this easy. GrowLog is not a suicide prevention app and need not offer all six, but it must get the numbers right.
usable.note: Martinengo et al., BMC Medicine 2019 matches: 6/69 (9%), two apps with over a million downloads each, and 5/69 (7%) with all six strategies. All six strategy percentages match. Two nuances: the 67% is direct access to a crisis helpline, and 94% of apps gave some emergency contact information. The authors notified developers, and two popular apps later fixed the errors.

usable.claim: The population line 'in trials' fits Linardon only. The second review also included nonrandomised and observational studies of adults with unipolar depression or bipolar disorder.
usable.values: Deterioration OR 0.79 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.01). Monitoring features 69.4% vs 51.1%. Mood worsening 0.02 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.02) from only 4 studies, not robust. Overall AE 0.04 (I2 80%). Causality not established.
usable.source: Linardon et al., npj Digital Medicine 2024. Astill Wright and colleagues, JMIR Mental Health 2025: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12548826/
usable.population: People pre-selected for mental health problems, in trials. Not healthy users of a consumer tracker.
usable.implication: The evidence does not show that apps harm people on average, but it is thin and a minority may do worse. Give users a way to pause logging, hide scores and reset, and ask occasionally whether tracking is helping. Since GrowLog has no server, these checks stay local and the team will not see harm rates, so be honest that safety data is not being collected.
usable.note: Linardon et al. matches: 171 trials, 55 reporting adverse events, 6.7% from 13 app conditions, 10.1% from 8 control conditions, and OR 0.79 (0.62 to 1.01) from 9 comparisons. The authors warn this is not conclusive evidence of no harm. The 69.4% vs 51.1% is the share of app conditions with monitoring in reporting vs non-reporting trials. Astill Wright et al. matches on 0.04, 0.04 and 0.02. The paper's Results give overall as 0.042 (I2 80.2%) and say the mood-worsening figure comes from 4 of 77 nonrandomised studies. Only 15 of 77 studies reported adverse events.

usable.claim: A strengths-based tone was a participant wish that the authors say may not always be possible. The formal recommendation is to co-design feedback tone with users.
usable.values: Distress appeared mostly temporary. The recommendations were not checked by Delphi and are interim. They suggest limiting app feedback on mood itself in research settings.
usable.source: Astill Wright et al., npj Digital Medicine 2025. Recommendations (Astill Wright et al., JMIR Mental Health 2026): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13229395/
usable.population: 457 participants, mostly adults with unipolar depression, over 3 to 12 months or hypothetical use. Not healthy adults or students.
usable.implication: Default to calm trend views. Lead with what helped, such as restful days and recovery activity. Make scores hideable, avoid red warning styling, and do not phrase personal thresholds as countdowns. Never use wording that implies a coming collapse. Let people skip days without penalty.
usable.note: The npj paper matches on 14 studies, 457 participants, self-trust, foreboding, rumination, health anxiety, obsessive checking, the preferences, and temporary rather than persistent distress. Bipolar depression was excluded, one sample was youth and three were mixed. The paper is internally inconsistent: its abstract says mixed-methods while its inclusion criteria say qualitative, and it gives 7 actual-use plus 6 hypothetical studies, with the Discussion saying 6/11. The JMIR 2026 paper confirms no Delphi, interim status, user control, toggling off intrusive functions, and limiting feedback on mood in research.

usable.claim: In a randomised study of 90 university students, seven days of ten-a-day prompts about positive or negative emotions did not change emotions or depressive symptoms in a condition-specific way. Separately, a review of 8 RCTs found no robust effect of mood monitoring on symptoms in bipolar disorder or depression, in either direction.
usable.values: Depression at 12 months SMD -0.25 (95% CI -0.49 to 0.00, 2 comparisons). Mania SMD -0.16 (CI -0.34 to 0.01). The review's abstract and results differ on the sign of the mania effect.
usable.source: De Vuyst, Dejonckheere, Van der Gucht, Kuppens, PLOS ONE 2019. Review in JMIR Mental Health 2026: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12779106/
usable.population: Students aged 18 to 24, 7 days. The review covers 1,230 people with bipolar disorder or depression.
usable.implication: Simple rating is unlikely to harm most students in the short term, and the same evidence means GrowLog cannot claim tracking reduces stress or symptoms. Say it helps you notice patterns. No study I found tests months of daily tracking in healthy adults.
usable.note: De Vuyst et al. matches: 90 students, 30 per condition, 10 prompts a day for 7 days. Affect did not change. PHQ-9 fell in all conditions including control, then returned to baseline at one month. The review matches on 8 RCTs and 1,230 people, and its abstract concludes no increase or decrease in bipolar disorder and no robust evidence in unipolar depression. The -0.25 figure is from unipolar trials only (n=262, P=.05, borderline). Mania is 0.16 in the abstract and -0.16 in the results, with the same CI, so the abstract's sign looks like a typo. The bipolar depression P value also conflicts with its CI.

usable.claim: False feedback can change how people feel and perform. In 63 adults with insomnia randomised to sham positive or negative sleep feedback, the negative group reported lower alert cognition and more sleepiness by evening, though vigilance and attentional bias did not differ. In 164 people, assigned sleep quality rather than self-rated sleep predicted some cognitive tests.
usable.values: Alert cognition d = 0.79, sleepiness or fatigue d = 0.55, attentional bias d = 0.20, vigilance d = 0.12. Commentary notes Draganich study 1 had no no-feedback baseline.
usable.source: Gavriloff et al., Journal of Sleep Research 2018 (abstract only). Draganich and Erdal, JEP:LMC 2014: https://www.noigroup.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Draganich_2014_sleep-fatigue-beliefs.pdf . Commentary: https://www.bps.org.uk/research-digest/placebo-sleep-can-boost-your-mental-performance
usable.population: Adults with DSM-5 insomnia disorder, and US college students. Single-exposure experiments about sleep, not burnout scores.
usable.implication: A number such as 82/100 presented as an objective reading is not neutral. Show the score as a summary of what the user entered, with its uncertainty. Avoid sending bad-news summaries first thing in the morning. No study I found directly tests telling someone they are burned out, so this is an extrapolation.
usable.note: The PubMed abstract matches for Gavriloff: 63 adults (32 negative, 31 positive) with DSM-5 insomnia and all four effect sizes. No objective performance difference appeared in that study, so the 'perform' half rests on Draganich. I read the Draganich and Erdal PDF (JEP:LMC 2014): 164 Colorado College undergraduates across two experiments, 50 and 114. Assigned sleep quality predicted PASAT and COWAT, but not Digit Span or SDMT, and SDMT was an unexpected null. The BPS commentary confirms the missing baseline in study 1 and suggests a possible nocebo reading.

usable.claim: In the DISCOVER trial, automated feedback after web depression screening was not associated with misdiagnosis, mistreatment, or worsening depression or emotional response. One signal appeared: non-tailored feedback raised worsening suicidal ideation at one month compared with no feedback, while tailored feedback did not, and this did not hold in the worst-case sensitivity analysis or at six months.
usable.values: Non-tailored RR 1.92 (95% CI 1.14 to 3.24) at 1 month; rates 12.3% vs 8.1% tailored vs 6.4% none. Worst-case ITT RR 1.26 (0.99 to 1.61). Post hoc, not powered. Some printed CIs for the tailored arm are inconsistent.
usable.source: Sikorski et al., Potential Harms of Feedback After Web-Based Depression Screening, J Med Internet Res 2025
usable.population: German adults with PHQ-9 of 10 or more and no recent diagnosis or treatment. 1,178 randomised, 948 per protocol.
usable.implication: A generic message of the form 'your score is high, see a professional' is the form to avoid. Base the prompt on what the person actually logged, such as several short-sleep days, and include supportive information and contacts. Evidence is limited and the result is exploratory.
usable.note: Sikorski et al., JMIR 2025 matches on 1,178 randomised, 948 per protocol, and the misdiagnosis, mistreatment, depression and emotional-response results. Rates of 12.3%, 8.1% and 6.4%, RR 1.92 (1.14 to 3.24) and worst-case RR 1.26 (0.99 to 1.61, P=.07) all match. Six-month nontailored RR was 1.12 (0.69 to 1.80). It is a post hoc analysis, unpowered, with no multiple-testing correction and a maximum of 39 events per arm. The tailored 1-month RR is 1.26 with a printed CI of 0.25 to 1.94, which is inconsistent and repeats a CI printed elsewhere. The authors say they cannot rule out an increase after nontailored feedback.

usable.claim: NICE NG225, as reported in a British Journal of Psychiatry editorial, tells mental health professionals not to use risk assessment tools and scales, or low, medium and high stratification, to predict future self-harm or suicide, or to decide who receives care. The stated reasons are poor positive predictive value, false reassurance, and exclusion of people rated lower risk.
