usable.source: Mughal et al., New guidance for self-harm: an opportunity not to be missed, BJPsych 2023. NICE's own pages returned 403 to my fetch, so this is a secondary report.
usable.population: People who self-harm, in clinical care in England.
usable.implication: Do not gate crisis contacts behind a score, and do not show bands that could read as 'you are safe'. A 1 to 5 mood log cannot assess suicide risk. Keep help visible for all users at all times. Any load level labels should describe the logged week, never the person's risk.
usable.note: Mughal et al. matches on professionals not using tools, scales or low, medium and high stratification, on treatment and discharge decisions, and on the three reasons. The authors were NG225 committee members. NICE's page also returned 403 to me, so this remains a secondary report. It concerns clinical care, not consumer apps, so applying it to GrowLog is an analogy.

usable.claim: A meta-analysis of 18 studies found that asking research participants about suicide did not increase risk and was linked to a small reduction in ideation and a lower likelihood of suicidal behaviour. Adolescents showed nearly twice the reduction seen in adults.
usable.values: Ideation g = -0.13. Behaviour OR = 0.714.
usable.source: Blades et al., Clinical Psychology Review 2018 (abstract only). Supporting review: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/does-asking-about-suicide-and-related-behaviours-induce-suicidal-ideation-what-is-the-evidence/FCAEE9E5BC840D76CF10AEBECD921AC9 (seen in search only, not opened).
usable.population: Research participants, not app users, and with human research oversight.
usable.implication: Plain language about hard moments is unlikely to cause harm, so the team need not hide the topic. The findings do not transfer directly to an unsupervised app, and an unattended question that scores risk runs into S3. Prefer an always-available '많이 힘들어요' button leading straight to contacts over a scored daily question.
usable.note: The PubMed abstract for Blades et al. 2018 matches: 18 studies, g = -0.13, OR = 0.714, and adolescents with nearly twice the reduction in ideation. I also opened the Cambridge page, which is Dazzi et al. 2014, an editorial-style review of 13 studies finding no significant increase in ideation. It is weaker than a meta-analysis. Neither covers an unsupervised consumer app.

usable.claim: Urgent suicide crisis is an exclusion from the voucher because psychiatric care comes first. The page describes eligible people as 국민 and sets no explicit residence test, so 'Korean residents' is imprecise.
usable.values: Against semistructured interviews: sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.92), specificity 0.85 (0.82 to 0.88).
usable.source: Levis et al., BMJ 2019 (abstract only). MOHW voucher page, last updated 2026-01-09: https://www.mohw.go.kr/menu.es?mid=a10706040800
usable.population: 58 studies, 17,357 participants, 2,312 with major depression. The voucher applies to Korean residents.
usable.implication: This is the best-grounded help-seeking line, but it belongs to the PHQ-9, not to GrowLog's ratings, and showing it conflicts with S8 and S9. Do not map GrowLog scores to it. Point users to real next steps instead: 지역 정신건강복지센터, 대학 상담센터, 심리상담 바우처, 정신건강의학과.
usable.note: The PubMed abstract for Levis et al. matches. The 0.88 and 0.85 figures come from the semistructured-interview subset of 29 studies and 6,725 participants, not all 58 studies. The MOHW page (updated 2026-01-09) confirms PHQ-9 of 10 or more from a national screening result within one year, 8 sessions, and no age or income criterion, though the co-payment varies by income. Referrers also include youth counselling centres and Wee centres, and private counselling centres are excluded. Psychiatric institutions supply a doctor's diagnosis or opinion within 3 months. 'Korea uses the same line' is a fair observation, but the page does not cite Levis.

usable.claim: WHO's fact sheet says episodes last "most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks", which is stricter than 'much of the day on most days'.
usable.values: Pooled screening sensitivity 0.86, specificity 0.81 (18 studies). Clinically relevant change about 10 points. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. Korean study used a cut-off of 13.
usable.source: WHO WHO-5 document 2024. WHO depression fact sheet, updated 2026-09-11: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/depression/ . Topp et al. 2015: https://karger.com/pps/article/84/3/167/282903/The-WHO-5-Well-Being-Index-A-Systematic-Review-of . Korean version 2010: https://scholar.kyobobook.co.kr/article/detail/4010023183248
usable.population: 213 articles across many populations. Korean evidence found only in 244 adults over 65.
usable.implication: No validated cut-off exists for GrowLog's 1 to 5 daily ratings, so any trigger is a convention. A defensible rule is low ratings on most logged days over about 14 days, labelled internally as a convention borrowed from a duration criterion. An optional periodic WHO-5 is positively worded and easier to justify than PHQ-9, but check licence terms, the Korean version, and its adult Korean validity first.
usable.note: The WHO-5 document (WHO/UCN/MSD/MHE/2024.1) confirms below 50 or raw below 13, further assessment, and CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. The percentage score is raw times four, so 50 cannot occur and '<50', '≤50' and raw '<13' pick out the same people. The licence also requires citation, no WHO endorsement or logo, same-licence adaptations and a translation disclaimer, and commercial use needs a WHO request. Topp et al. confirms 213 articles, ≤50, 0.86 and 0.81 from 18 studies, and 10 points. The Korean study confirms 244 people over 65 and below 13, and gives no accuracy figures in what I saw. 'Found only' is a search-limited negative I could not recheck because the search budget ran out. The fact sheet date of 2026-09-11 is shown but not labelled as an update date.

usable.claim: In real-world panel data on 93 popular Android mental health apps, median day-30 retention was 3.3% and median daily open rate 4.0%. Tracker apps did somewhat better, at 6.1% retention and 6.3% daily opens.
usable.values: Day 15 median 3.9% (IQR 10.3%). Day 30 median 3.3% (IQR 6.2%). Peer support 8.9%, breathing 0.0%.
usable.source: Baumel, Muench, Edan, Kane, J Med Internet Res 2019 (PubMed abstract only; the JMIR page returned no content)
usable.population: Users of 93 Android apps with 10,000 or more installs, targeting anxiety, depression or emotional wellbeing.
usable.implication: Most users will never produce enough data for personal thresholds, and very few will log a real burnout event. Defaults must work on day 1, and personal adjustment should need few inputs and improve gradually. State how many days the estimate rests on. Do not treat those who stay as representative when judging whether the method works.
usable.note: The PubMed abstract for Baumel et al. 2019 matches, including 'panel' data, 93 apps, 10,000+ installs, 3.9%, 3.3%, 4.0%, 6.1%, 6.3% and 0.0%. The peer-support 8.9% rests on only 2 apps, and tracker day-30 retention has a wide IQR of 20.4%.

usable.claim: Only uptake and attrition have very wide prediction intervals. Adherence's interval is 53.2% to 69.7%.
usable.values: Liu: uptake 92.4%, adherence 61.8%, posttest attrition 18.6%, follow-up 28.4%, with very wide prediction intervals. Jabs: stress d = 0.28, depression d = 0.25, anxiety d = 0.22; personalisation F(1,44) = 6.10, p = .017.
usable.source: Liu et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2026 (abstract only). Jabs et al., Early Intervention in Psychiatry 2026: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13406923/
usable.population: RCT participants with depression or anxiety, and university students across 122 studies (N = 21,504). Trial users are far more engaged than ordinary downloaders.
usable.implication: Do not rely on streaks or badges. The evidence for gamification is weak but leans against it, and missed streaks may also add guilt. Reminders are optional and low cost. Personalisation has some support, in intervention trials rather than threshold tuning. These effects are from active programmes, so they do not support claiming benefit for a tracker.
usable.note: The JAMA abstract for Liu et al. matches on 79 RCTs and the moderators. It was published online 2025-11-19, in the 2026 volume. The Key Points box differs from the abstract Results (94%, 62%, 17%, 27%), so cite the Results figures. Jabs et al. confirms university students, 122 studies, N = 21,504, attrition 17.0%, adherence 70.0%, all three d values and F(1,44) = 6.10, p = .017. No examined characteristic, reminders included, was associated with attrition. The meta-analyses use 68 RCTs, and adherence rests on 29 estimates from 26 studies. The two reviews conflict on reminders.

usable.claim: Morrison does not show daily notifications led to more viewing: d = .44 with a CI of -.15 to 1.01, and the authors treat it as tentative. Stone does not say users cannot log when low; its nearest example is people in high pain being disinclined to answer. Avoiding self-reflection when low is reported by Astill Wright et al. 2025 (S15).
usable.values: RR 1.039 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.08); largest at 12:30 (8.8%). Morrison ceased use within 2 weeks: 42% daily, 39% occasional, 60% intelligent (up to 3 a day). Stone: little evidence that mood or stress affects compliance, but skipped moments are unobserved, and some users say they cannot log when low.
usable.source: Wrzus and Neubauer, Assessment 2023. Morrison et al., PLOS ONE 2017: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5207732/ . Bidargaddi et al., JMIR mHealth 2018: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6293241/ . Stone et al., Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 2022: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12991416/
usable.population: Paid or motivated research participants (median 7 days) and employees. Morrison was underpowered and Bidargaddi disclosed company ties.
usable.implication: Offer at most one daily reminder, off by default or at a time the user picks, with a long logging window. A PWA's notifications are also less reliable, so do not depend on them. Do not treat missing days as good days or as bad days: leave them blank and exclude them from thresholds. Do not send notifications about high scores.
usable.note: Wrzus and Neubauer matches on 477 articles, 79.19% and no link to compliance or dropout. It has 496 samples and a median of 7 days, and only 33% of studies reported monetary incentives. It was published online in 2022. Bidargaddi matches on 1,255 users, RR 1.039 (1.01 to 1.08), 12:30 at 8.8%, and disclosed company ties. Morrison matches on 77 usable of 162 randomised, and on the 42%, 39% and 60% figures. Stone matches on little evidence of mood or stress affecting compliance and on skipped moments being unobserved; its printed date is 2022 Dec 7, with a 2023 issue date.

usable.claim: The official Korean BAT file credits no translator and states no terms of its own. Its wording matches Cho's translation before item 9 was dropped. Cho reports translating through the authors' BAT consortium and is listed as its South Korea member. No source says whether Cho or KSIOP hold rights in the Korean wording.
usable.values: Official file: 3 pages, 23 core items (exhaustion 1-8, mental distance 9-13, cognitive 14-18, emotional 19-23) plus 10 secondary items numbered 1-10, one 5-point frequency scale, no time frame, no reverse-scored items, footer citing the 2019 Test Manual. Cho's article page shows CC BY-NC 4.0.
usable.source: KU Leuven, BAT-Korean.pdf; Cho S (2020), Korean J Ind Organ Psychol 33(4):461-499; Consortium-Members-2026 list on the official site.
usable.population: Not applicable (instrument file).
usable.implication: The KU Leuven terms cover use without permission, but the Korean wording's rights holder is unstated. Ask Cho before a wide launch.
usable.note: Checked item by item by number only; no wording copied. The skeptic confirmed the match and the consortium role, and found no permission statement either way.

usable.claim: BAT-12 is the authors' own short form, marked with asterisks on items 1, 3, 4, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 23 of both the English and Korean work forms. The user manual prefers the full version for individual assessment; the test manual allows BAT-12 for screening and monitoring.
usable.values: BAT-12 pooled lines 2.54 (.89/.79) and 2.96 (.71/.89); the Finnish manual gives 3.04 (specificity .92). The 2022 BAT-12 paper lists EX5 instead of EX3 in one sentence, an internal error; take the set from the official form.
usable.source: Schaufeli, De Witte, Desart, User Manual and Test Manual v2.0 (2020); Hadzibajramovic, Schaufeli, De Witte (2022), BAT-12 paper; Schaufeli et al. (2023).
usable.population: European workers.
usable.implication: Using exactly the 12 starred items is not a modification. GrowLog uses BAT-23 because individual feedback is its use and the BAT-23 lines agree across sources.
usable.note: Corrects the earlier model-spec line that lumped BAT-12 with self-chosen subsets.

usable.claim: The BAT total core score is the sum of all core items divided by their number, rounded to two decimals; subscales are the mean of their own items. No manual or cut-off paper gives a missing-item rule.
usable.values: The 2023 pooled paper does not describe missing-data handling. The Swedish cut-off study used complete answers only.
usable.source: Schaufeli, De Witte, Desart, User Manual and Test Manual v2.0 (2020); Schaufeli et al. (2023); Swedish cut-off study (sources I13).
usable.population: Not applicable.
usable.implication: Score only complete checks. Prorating would be a product choice with no source.
usable.note: The scoring skeptic could not confirm complete-case handling for the 2023 paper; only the Swedish study states it.

usable.claim: Cho (2020) is a preliminary validation in Korean office workers. Item 9 (mental distance) loaded poorly and was dropped, leaving 22 items in four factors. The second-order model fitted worse than four correlated factors, and Cho suggests subscale scores may be more appropriate than one total.
usable.values: Study 1: 367 office workers (EFA). Study 2: 345 workers at one public corporation (CFA). Alphas .84 to .94. CFA TLI .893, AVE .404. Mean 2.46 (SD .62) on 22 items. No omega, test-retest, norms or cut-offs. Cho calls for item 9 to be re-translated.
usable.source: Cho S (2020). A Preliminary Validation Study for the Korean version of the Burnout Assessment Tool (K-BAT). Korean J Ind Organ Psychol 33(4):461-499. doi:10.24230/kjiop.v33i4.461-499
usable.population: South Korean office workers.
usable.implication: The 23-item Korean total has no Korean psychometric evidence. Use it only because the European lines were set on 23 items, and say so.
usable.note: Korean studies citing K-BAT used 22, 23+10, 12 and 10 items and different scorings, so their numbers are not comparable.

usable.claim: From the test manual's SD .64 and alpha .96, the individual measurement error is about .13 (95% interval about ±.25) and a reliable change needs about .36. Using the 6-month retest r .74 instead gives about .90. The manual's own example uses SE .02, which is the standard error of the mean, not of an individual score.
usable.values: SEm = .64 × √(1 − .96) ≈ .128; RC = 1.96 × √2 × SEm ≈ .36. With r .74: SEm ≈ .33, RC ≈ .90. 1-month Japanese r .64 and 6-month Flemish r .74 come from different samples.
usable.source: Schaufeli, De Witte, Desart, Test Manual v2.0 (2020), Tables 11 and 60; arithmetic by the researcher.
usable.population: Flemish workers.
usable.implication: Do not report a month-to-month change smaller than .36. GrowLog uses .36 as a floor, the lenient end.
usable.note: No responsiveness or minimal important change study exists for the BAT.

usable.claim: The pooled 2023 lines are preliminary. The authors suggest provisional use in similar European countries and in countries where the BAT was validated, such as Japan; Korea is not listed. The case groups were partly self-reported.
usable.values: Cases: Dutch and Finnish clinically assessed groups, Flemish interviewed cases plus 91 online respondents reporting a recent professional diagnosis; 542 cases against 4,145 workers. Sweden's own lines are lower (2.41, 2.80). The user manual says lines should preferably come from national samples.
usable.source: Schaufeli WB, De Witte H, Hakanen JJ, Kaltiainen J, Kok R (2023). How to assess severe burnout? Cutoff points for the BAT based on three European samples. Scand J Work Environ Health 49(4):293-302. doi:10.5271/sjweh.4093
usable.population: Workers in the Netherlands, Flanders and Finland.
usable.implication: Show the lines as provisional European lines with no Korean calibration, never as a diagnosis.
usable.note: Korean studies that applied European lines (one hospital's nurses, one surgeon group) have unreconciled tables or unstated cut-offs and are not cited in the app.

gaps: Search stopped early: the shared WebSearch budget ran out, so the last three searches did not run (OLBI test-retest, primary source of OLBI cutoffs, minimal important difference for MBI and CBI). I continued with direct fetches of already known URLs only. Absence of these items below means not reached, not proven absent.

No minimal important change or responsiveness study was found for any burnout measure, and no study validating weekly or monthly repetition of MBI, CBI, OLBI, BAT or SMBM. Figueiredo 2024 states this for SMBM; Shoman 2021 reports it for five measures.
No validated Korean short daily or weekly exhaustion measure was found. OLBI day-level evidence is Polish; the single fatigue item is Dutch.

No burnout measure validated in self-employed, freelance or gig workers was found in one search, and the BAT Test Manual text has no mention of self-employment. All norms and cutoffs here come from employees or patients.

No official OLBI licence statement was found from Demerouti or the publisher. Secondary sites calling it free are not authoritative. Primary OLBI cutoff papers were not opened; the values come from one arXiv paper's methods section.
No Korean OLBI validation was found. Korean-language journals may not have been reached by the search tool.
No Korean norms or cutoffs for BAT, CBI or PSS from a representative sample were found. It is unverified whether the Korean PDF on the BAT site matches Cho (2020)'s 22-item form.

KBOSS development paper (Kim HD et al. 2021, Saf Health Work 12(4):522-529, doi 10.1016/j.shaw.2021.08.001) could not be opened (403 and certificate errors). Search-result text only: n=444, alpha .813, cutoffs 21, 18 and 15 at the upper quartile. Excluded from claims. Its licence is unknown.

Kristensen et al. 2005 (Work & Stress) returned 403, so CBI test-retest and sensitivity-to-change figures were not read. The NFA page mentions a PhD thesis with three-year follow-up, also not read. Kristensen's 2019 information sheet on cut-points was not opened.

JMIR Formative Research 2026 e92458 (daily exhaustion EMA with monthly BAT, 18 people on sick leave) rendered empty on three URLs; seen only as search text, so excluded. It looks directly relevant and should be read by hand.

MBI test-retest figures were not found; the manual is paid. Korean MBI validation: Shin et al. 2011 (MBI-SS, Asia Pacific Educ Rev 12:633-639) was confirmed at abstract level at https://scholar.korea.ac.kr/handle/2021.sw.korea/111108 but left out because the MBI cannot be embedded. A Korean MBI-GS citation was not verified.

PSS: the ePROVIDE page rendered empty and Mind Garden's PSS URL returned 404, so the actual fee and whether a free app counts as profit-making are unknown until a request is filed. The FAQ's nominal fee has no amount. No PSS Korean translator terms were found.

Whether NFA's permission extends to rewording CBI for students, translation, or the CBI-K wording is unstated. No student CBI validation was opened; the Italian paper at PMC6121611 used client wording without validating it.

Left out for space (opened): Rotenstein 2018 JAMA, at least 142 burnout definitions and 0% to 80.5% prevalence in physicians, https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2702871 ; De Beer 2024 MBI-GS meta-analysis, structural and cross-cultural validity unclear, https://research-portal.uu.nl/en/publications/maslach-burnout-inventory-general-survey-a-systematic-review-and-/ ; Warttig 2013 PSS-4 English sample n=1,568, norm values not on the page, https://research.edgehill.ac.uk/en/publications/new-normative-english-sample-data-for-the-short-form-perceived-st/ .

No validated population cut-off was found for daily 1-5 ratings of stress, energy or mood. Diary research uses within-person scores, so any rating threshold in the app will be a design convention.

No defensible daily-hours threshold for burnout was found, and no evidence on the required number of rest days per week.

Student evidence is thin: no longitudinal study of study hours and burnout, and nothing specific to Korean students' study time. The PISA finding is cross-sectional, in 15-year-olds, and concerns life satisfaction.

No study applied critical slowing down or early-warning statistics to burnout. The depression evidence seen was preprint abstracts; Kunkels 2023 and the published Helmich paper were blocked (HTTP 403).

Accumulation versus reactivity: multi-day stressor pile-up (Grzywacz and Almeida 2008) was seen only through secondary text, because the PMC article was blocked. No diary study showed daily reactivity or accumulation predicting burnout months later.

Population evidence does not transfer directly to one person. Almost all effects here are between-person averages from workers, midlife adults, clinical cohorts or health care staff, and developers specifically were not studied in any source. No source tested a personalised burnout threshold on self-logged data.

Search limit: the shared web search budget ran out before I could search these topics, so they have no claims: the Guthier et al. 2020 continuous-time meta-analysis of stressors and burnout (DOI resolved, abstract would not load), Ford et al. 2014 time lags (located, not opened), Oura Cumulative Stress, Garmin HRV Status and load windows, Apple Training Load, typical within-person SD and lag-1 autocorrelation of daily 1 to 5 ratings, and the relapse-signature literature. Recall bias: no claim. Neubauer et al. 2020 (end-of-day vs aggregated momentary affect) was located, but the PDF refused connection and the Penn State page returned 403. The search summary suggested fairly high convergence with small peak and recency biases for negative affect; I could not confirm that.

Response shift: no claim. Schwartz et al. 2006 and the 2023 and 2024 reviews could not be opened. Search summaries gave d about .08 to .32 and medians about .20 to .30, unverified. I found nothing on response shift in daily burnout ratings, so whether a person's meaning of '4 out of 5' drifts over months remains unknown.

Personal burnout labels: I found no study where individuals mark their own burnout events and a model learns from them. All event evidence here is borrowed from schizophrenia relapse and depression recurrence. Whether self-marked burnout can be dated accurately is unknown.
Minimum events: no published minimum exists in what I found for one person's event threshold. The 3 and 5 event gates in I18 are my convention, and only the prediction-interval arithmetic is derived.

Days for a baseline: no source gives a day count for one daily 1 to 5 rating. The figures are extrapolated from ICCs and from momentary prompt data. I also found no published CUSUM or EWMA study on single-person daily burnout or stress ratings.

Simulation limits: the false alarm, delay and MAD figures in I6, I7 and I8 come from my own quick synthetic simulation (Gaussian AR(1) latent, mean 3, SD 0.8 unless noted, rounded to 1 to 5, SD floor 0.4, one-sided alarms, fixed baseline, 3,000 runs). They are design guidance, not validation.
SPC vs early warning signals: the claim that SPC outperformed signals comes from a project report with no numbers. The underlying paper was not identified or opened.
